St. Irenaeus says in the second century, in his interpretation of the saying of the prophecy "the kingdom shall be divided," and in his reference to the ten toes: "The ten toes, then, are the ten kings into whom the kingdom will be divided, and some of them will be strong and active, and others lazy and useless, but they will agree." And St. Jerome says: [He observes that the prophecy was fulfilled in his own time partly in the destruction of the empire by internal enmity and civil wars. It was fulfilled afterward in the division into an eastern empire and a western empire, and it was fulfilled finally in its division into many small provinces]. St. Hippolytus sees that the ten toes, of iron and of clay, mean the democracies that were rising and divided among the ten toes of the statue, in which the iron would be mixed with the clay.

g. Some see that the mixing of iron with clay signifies the mixing of the elements of two distinct civilizations, the entry of the barbarian peoples into the heart of the civilized empire and the barbarians' adoption of the forms of civilization. Hence the invasion of the Germanic tribes on the one hand and of the Turks on the other is an interpretation closer to the true meaning of the symbol in the prophecy.

"34 Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out without hands, which smote the image upon his feet that were of iron and clay, and brake them to pieces. 35 Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken to pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshingfloors; and the wind carried them away, that no place was found for them.
And the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth. 36 This is the dream; and we will tell the interpretation thereof before the king." [34-36].

The most important thing in the dream is this wonderful stone, able to shatter these kingdoms in order to establish a spiritual kingdom that fills the earth, a kingdom that stands forever. Here he speaks of a new kingdom established by the stone cut out without hands, for the Lord Christ came not from the seed of man, but born of the Virgin.
The expression "not by hands" points to the nature of His kingdom, that it is not human but heavenly and divine, with no beginning.

The Lord Christ is called the stone or the rock because He is the cornerstone who joined the Jews with the Gentiles in one faith, that is, He bound them together as two walls joined by the cornerstone. He is the stone upon which His Church is founded. It was said of Him:

"The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes" (Ps 118:22-23). The prophet Isaiah calls Him: "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the children of Israel" (Isa 8:14), and "a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation" (Isa 28:16). And the prophet Zechariah says: "For behold the stone that I have laid before Joshua; upon one stone shall be seven eyes" (Zech 3:9; see Acts 4:11; 1 Pet 2:7-8).

* After this it remains that "the stone comes from heaven, which smote the image (the statue) and terrified it and shattered all the kingdoms, and gives the Kingdom to the saints of the Most High God.
* The stone that smites the image and breaks it in pieces, which fills the whole earth, is Christ, who came from heaven and brought judgment upon the world.

St. Hippolytus of Rome * For this reason also, when Daniel saw His coming beforehand, he said that a stone cut out without hands comes into the world. For this is what "without hands" means, that His coming into this world is not accomplished by human work, that is, by the work of those who are accustomed to cut stones. Joseph had no part in it; Mary alone cooperated with the plan (divine) that had been prepared beforehand. This stone, which is from the earth, was found by the power and wisdom of God. Therefore Isaiah also says: "Behold, I lay in Zion a stone... a precious corner stone, a sure foundation" (Isa 28:16). Thus, then, we understand that His coming in human nature was not accomplished by the will of man but by the will of God.

St. Irenaeus * This mountain signifies the kingdom of the Jews, and from this mountain He was cut out, where Christ was born. When he says "without hands" we understand that it is without any human work, because works are known by the hands.
Father Caesarius * This is the temple of the body that was taken and cut out of the mountain of human nature and the substance of the body, and that without hands, that is, without the work of men.

Origen * A great stone was placed upon the well (Gen 29), where many shepherds were accustomed to roll it away when they came together, and then they would give water to themselves and to their flocks. But Jacob alone rolled the stone away and watered the flocks of his bride... What is this stone placed there but Christ Himself...? Daniel also says: "a stone cut out without hands," who is Christ, born without the (seed of a) man. It is a new and wonderful thing that a stone should be cut from the rock without an axe or tools for cutting stones; so, above all wonder, an offspring should appear from a virgin who had not married.
St. Gregory of Nyssa

37 "Thou, O king, art a king of kings: for the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, power, and strength, and glory. 38 And wheresoever the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven hath he given into thine hand, and hath made thee ruler over them all. Thou art this head of gold. 39 And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth. 40 And the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things: and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise. 41 And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters' clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay. 42 And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay, so the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken. 43 And whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay. 44 And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever. 45 Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter: and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure."
"This is the dream;
and we will tell the interpretation thereof before the king.

And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.
Forasmuch as thou sawest that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold;
the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter:
and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure." [36-45].

46 "Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours unto him. 47 The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret. 48 Then the king made Daniel a great man, and gave him many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon, and chief of the governors over all the wise men of Babylon."
"Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours unto him" [46].

It was no easy matter for Nebuchadnezzar to fall down and worship Daniel, he who counted himself like a god, to whom all men bow down; especially since Daniel had not brought him joyful news but had affirmed to him that his kingdom would pass away. Yet the king felt his great weakness before the work of God and His plan. The king bowed down in humility, glorifying the God of Daniel, but only for a time, as Pharaoh did before (Ex 9:27; 10:16). Nebuchadnezzar himself touched the mighty hand of God and bore witness to it and declared: "How great are the signs of the Most High God, and how mighty are His wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and His dominion is from generation to generation," but he lost this when he became bound to the love of vain glory, and in a life of luxury the thorns choked the word that had sprung up in him.
"The king answered unto Daniel, and said:
Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret" [47].

He glorified God, but only for a time, since he did not take serious steps for the salvation of his soul. God permitted this to encourage the captive Jews, that they might realize that God is able to be glorified in them if they return to Him with all their hearts.
"Then the king made Daniel a great man, and gave him many great gifts, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon, and chief of the governors over all the wise men of Babylon" [48].

Daniel accepted the king's gift for the sake of serving his people. For this reason he was concerned to appoint the three youths over the affairs of the province of Babylon, knowing that they desired nothing of the honors of this world and its wealth, but he did this for the sake of his brethren the captives.
"Then Daniel requested of the king, and he set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, over the affairs of the province of Babylon:
but Daniel sat in the gate of the king." [49].

Daniel was at the king's gate as head of the men of the palace, so that his eyes might watch every movement and every person entering the palace. Perhaps this meant that he took charge of judgment in matters that touched the royal palace, since it was the ancient custom that the places of judgment were set up at the gate of the palace.
Daniel and his companions did not desire temporal things, but sought the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and God gave them both.
* When they asked for heavenly things from the Lord, they received temporal things also from the king.
St. Hippolytus of Rome
Let me enter into my house!
* The king, his men, and his counselors were troubled because of a forgotten dream, but Daniel's soul was not shaken at being exposed to death unjustly!
Grant me to enter with Daniel into my house, that I may enter into my inner Jerusalem, to meet You, O God of heaven, with Your angels and Your saints.
* You carry me to Your eternal chamber, You reveal to me Your surpassing mysteries, and You grant me a knowledge that delights my soul.
Turn my life into a joyful hymn of praise!
Instead of being troubled by distress, let my whole being be shaken with rejoicing.
* I realize that all the kingdoms of the world are like a metal statue that is shattered.
You are the cornerstone; You shatter evil and gather the saints in Yourself!
You are the One who declares to the earth the abundance of Your love!
Let every statue foreign to You be shattered within me, and establish Your joyful Kingdom within me!

entries.section: 1. The setting up of a golden statue:

paragraphs.text: 1 "Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits: he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. 2 Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. 3 Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up. 4 Then an herald cried aloud, To you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages, 5 That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up: 6 And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. 7 Therefore at that time, when all the people heard the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and all kinds of musick, all the people, the nations, and the languages, fell down and worshipped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up."
"Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits: he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon" [1].

Some rabbis see that Nebuchadnezzar wanted to erase the effect of the dream upon the people throughout his kingdom, for he felt that many had glorified the God of Israel; therefore he set up this statue to occupy people's minds. Was this statue of Nebuchadnezzar himself, to set himself among the ranks of the gods, or of the god Bel, the chief god of the state, or of a new god? The prophet Daniel does not mention it. But the prevailing opinion is that he wanted to deify himself. For though he had humbled himself for a while before the prophet Daniel, love of vain glory and pride quickly rose up in him.

Perhaps after the matter of his dream spread, the king feared that the Jews would incite the nations not to worship the king's gods; so the king set up this statue as a test for all the peoples he had taken captive, whether they were subject to him and to his worship or not. He set it up in the plain of Dura, or in the open city.

Because of the enormous size of the statue, some critics thought the story was not historical. But the reply to this is that it is not necessary that the whole statue be of pure gold, but only overlaid with gold, and that the dimensions of the statue include the massive base on which the statue stood.

"Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.

Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the wise men of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. Then an herald cried aloud,

To you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages, that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up:
and whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace.

entries.section: 1. The setting up of a golden statue:

paragraphs.text: Therefore at that time, when all the people heard the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and all kinds of musick, all the people, the nations, and the languages, fell down and worshipped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up" [2-7].

The dimensions of the statue pointed to deficiency, for we know that the number 7 points to perfection, while the number 8 points to what is beyond temporal perfection (because time is made up of the 7 days of the week), as though the number 8 meant the transcending of time, and the Lord Christ rose on the first day of the new week, or the eighth of the previous week. The number 6, however, points to deficiency; therefore the name of the Antichrist is 666 (Rev 13:13-18), that is, certain deficiency. And the statue here was sixty cubits in height and six cubits in breadth [1].

Nebuchadnezzar used every means so that all would worship his statue. He used the army, with the great men advancing at the head of the ranks to terrify the common people, and he used every kind of music of that time to stir the emotions. So in every generation the enemy of good uses every means to draw us into worshipping him by one means or another, or to turn men aside to the way of sin, and to count the holy life a life of rebellion against society.

The peoples bowed down to the statue, whether it was of Bel or of the king or of another god, not in a spirit of piety but by the command of the king, who threatened not only with death but with torture, where the disobedient would be cast into a furnace of fire.

entries.section: 2. A complaint against the three youths:

paragraphs.text: The wicked spoke to the king with flattery and hypocrisy, ascribing to the faithful and godly youths ingratitude and disobedience toward the king and his commands, but the youths had learned that God must be obeyed rather than men (Acts 5:29).
"8 Wherefore at that time certain Chaldeans came near, and accused the Jews. 9 They spake and said to the king Nebuchadnezzar,

O king, live for ever. 10 Thou, O king, hast made a decree, that every man that shall hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, shall fall down and worship the golden image: 11 And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth, that he should be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. 12 There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego;
these men, O king, have not regarded thee:
they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up." [8-12].

Note here the use of some Greek musical instruments, for Greek culture had influenced the region through the spread of Greek merchants and the presence of Greek colonies before the rise of the Greek Empire.

It is clear from the text that the movements of the youths were under strict watch, especially after the command to worship the statue was issued. Perhaps some of the king's counselors told him that these men of foreign race did not join the rest of the men of the palace in the Babylonian religious rites, these whom the king had raised from slavery to occupy great positions in the state. Because of envy, the accusation was made against these godly men that they were ungrateful, rebellious, and not worshippers of the gods.

We should not wonder that the Chaldeans, whom Daniel and his three companions had rescued from certain death (Dan 2:2), came to the king complaining against those who had saved them, so that he might cast the three youths into the furnace of fire, thus repaying them love with hatred, and kindness with envy and a desire to be rid of them. For ingratitude is the nature of fallen man, and persecution is the mark of the wicked; they trouble the righteous without cause.

St. Clement of Rome says: [You find nowhere in the Holy Scriptures that the righteous were cast out by the holy. Truly we find in them righteous men persecuted by the wicked, good men imprisoned by the wretched, and just men stoned by the lawless and killed by men under wrath, who bore them envy and spite; but they bore such sufferings with glory. What shall I say, brethren? Was Daniel cast into the lions' den by men who feared God?! Were Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael cast into the furnace of fire by men who worshipped the Most High in a glorious and great manner?! Far be it from us to have this thought!].

"13 Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Then they brought these men before the king. 14 Nebuchadnezzar spake and said unto them, Is it of purpose, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that ye do not serve my gods, nor worship the golden image which I have set up? 15 Now if ye be ready that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the image which I have made; well: but if ye worship not, ye shall be cast the same hour into the midst of a burning fiery furnace; and who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands? 16 Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter. 17 If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. 18 But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up."
"Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Then they brought these men before the king.
Nebuchadnezzar spake and said unto them,
Is it of purpose, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that ye do not serve my gods, nor worship the golden image which I have set up?

Now if ye be ready that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the image which I have made; well:
but if ye worship not, ye shall be cast the same hour into the midst of a burning fiery furnace;
and who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands?" [13-15].
Nothing provokes those in authority like the feeling that their authority is despised. They demand that all obey their commands even if they are unjust.
Having calmed a little, he gave them a last chance to save their lives, if they would bow down to the statue just once!
What concerned him was not whether they bowed to the statue or not, but their defiance of his authority; therefore he mocked their God, saying that He could not deliver them out of his hand.
"Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, answered and said to the king,
O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter.
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up" [16-18].

The scholar Tertullian speaks of obedience to kings and rulers (Rom 13:1; 1 Pet 2:13-14) in everything except what touches the faith, saying: [For this reason also the three brethren were set forth as an example for us, who were obedient to Nebuchadnezzar in other matters, and with all firmness refused to honor the statue].
The youths could have found excuses by which to justify bowing down to the statue, among them:
a. They were young in age, and captives.
b. They were under the authority of a violent king.
c. The king held absolute authority, especially over them as prisoners of war. They were asked to bow down even once without being prevented from worshipping God.
d. Every kind of music was offered to influence them.
e. The king himself, who had granted them the blessings in which they lived in the palace, entered into the dialogue with them and began to threaten them.
f. They were in a foreign land, easily exposed to accusation. And in exile how easy it is to apply the saying: "When in Rome do as the Romans do."

g. Their forefathers in Jerusalem and all Judah and Israel worshipped idols even inside the very temple of the Lord, as is stated in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and without external pressure, whereas these strangers insisted not to bow down to a statue in a foreign land.

h. By refusing to bow down to idols they were exposed to death, and so would lose every opportunity to play any part in working on behalf of their people. This is a purely human measure, which the young men rejected in a spirit of faith, trusting in God who works for their good and is able to deliver them if He so wills.
The furnace was of red brick, with an opening at the top, and it also had a side door through which the king saw the youths and with them the one like the son of the gods.

In the dialogue King Nebuchadnezzar challenged their God, while they defied death for the sake of their faithfulness to God. They believed that their God is able to save them, and if He did not save them from the temporal fire, this did not mean their betrayal of Him. They did not care about the king's threats, relying in their perseverance upon their living faith:
a. They believed that God is able to save them, and that He is the guardian of their lives, and that He would not permit their death if that were of benefit to them.
b. They believed that if He permitted them to die, they would accept it with courage, offering their lives as a sacrifice of love to God.

By this these youths are counted martyrs, because they bore witness to the divine truth, offering their lives as the price of witness, regardless of whether they were killed or the Lord rescued them from death. As St. Augustine says, martyrdom is not accomplished by the means of death, but by the state of the believer. For martyrdom rests on two principles: the first is faith in God as the keeper of our life and its leader to where He wishes, and the second is the opening of a door in heaven before our eyes so that we may see the glory prepared for us, looking upon our life here as a temporary passing.

* Look at their faith! They say: We believe that He is able to save us, but if our sins prevent Him, we believe in Him who does not wish to hand us over (to eternal death). We do not believe in this life but in the life to come. And we do not believe in Him so that we may escape burning here, but so that we may not escape passing through this fire and fall into another fire. So do what you wish, prepare your furnace, with this heat of it and its fire, for it is for our purification.
St. Jerome Perhaps some will ask: Why was no complaint made against Daniel that he did not bow down to the statue?
The answer to this is:
First: Perhaps Daniel was on a mission outside the region.

Second: Perhaps the accusers feared that the king would stand against them, because they knew his esteem for Daniel and how he had bowed down to him; therefore they wanted to focus on the three youths as Daniel's helpers, and perhaps it was in their plan to accuse him after being rid of these youths.
Third: Perhaps this was not demanded of Daniel, because the king felt that he himself ought to bow down to Daniel, for he is greater than the statue or on its level.

entries.section: 4. The casting of the youths into the furnace:

paragraphs.text: "19 Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated. 20 And he commanded the most mighty men that were in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. 21 Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. 22 Therefore because the king's commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. 23 And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell down bound into the midst of the burning fiery furnace." [19-23].
They were cast into the furnace from the upper opening.
By looking to the eternal fire they did not fear the temporal fire, nor dread death (Lk 12:4-5). For what did the fires of persecution do to them?
a. The Word of God appeared (like the son of the gods), He who was within them, appeared to embrace and protect them.
b. The flames loosed the bonds, but could not touch a hair of their body or the edge of their garment.

entries.section: 4. The casting of the youths into the furnace:

paragraphs.text: c. The king acknowledged their God, the Savior of His believers, and honored them in the province of Babylon [30].
St. John Cassian sees that the king of Babylon here signifies Satan, who stirs up within us the furnace of the fire of passions through gluttony.

* Being kept by this zeal of mind and continual contrition, we strike the dangerous passions of the flesh by depriving it (of the foods that stir it toward arrogance and pride); and thus by the abundance of our tears and the weeping of our hearts we succeed in quenching the flame of the furnace of our flesh, which the Babylonian king kindles (Dan 3:6), and which he continually feeds with occasions of sin and destructive vices. In this, by the grace of God, the dew can descend into our hearts by His Spirit, and the heat of the fleshly passions can be completely destroyed.
St. John Cassian
"24 Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was astonied, and rose up in haste, and spake, and said unto his counsellors,
Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?

They answered and said unto the king, True, O king. 25 He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. 26 Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace, and spake, and said,
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, ye servants of the most high God, come forth, and come hither.

Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, came forth of the midst of the fire. 27 And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them. 28 Then Nebuchadnezzar spake, and said,

Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants that trusted in him, and have changed the king's word, and yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God. 29 Therefore I make a decree, That every people, nation, and language, which speak any thing amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, shall be cut in pieces, and their houses shall be made a dunghill: because there is no other God that can deliver after this sort. 30 Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in the province of Babylon." [24-30].
The furnace had a side door, at which the king stood at a distance to see them as they were cast in, one after another, and to watch them burning. But what did he see?
First: The flames proved them righteous in the eyes of God and the eyes of the king, and one like the Son of God appeared, glorifying them.
Second: The flames loosed the iron bonds and did not affect the clothes of the youths.
Third: While some of the soldiers who cast the youths in died because of the intensity of the heat, the youths were walking about.
Fourth: The flames turned into dew, and perhaps the king longed to enjoy what they were enjoying, but he could not enter in to them, but only called them to come out to him.
The youths did not come out of the furnace but kept walking about, until the command came to them from the king. They are obedient to him in the Lord.

The Chaldeans knew the story of the casting of the three youths into the furnace. They became a living witness, in the provinces of Babylon before all, of God the Savior of His godly ones and of the power of taking refuge in Him. But what did the king do regarding his eternity?!

* (By prayer) Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were found worthy to be heard, and to be fortified by the blowing of a wind that brought dew and prevented the effect of the flame of the fire upon them. And the mouths of the lions in the den of the Babylonians were stopped by the prayers of Daniel.

* Hananiah and his companions went down into a spiritual blessing granted to all the saints, which Isaac pronounced when he said to Jacob: "Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven" (Gen 27:28), greater than the physical dew that quenched the flame of Nebuchadnezzar?!

* Now too Nebuchadnezzar speaks the same words as ours, for we are the true Hebrews, Hebrews of the life to come (Heb 11:13); we experience the heavenly dew that quenches all fires from us, and with the same higher side of our souls we imitate these youths.

Origen * Truly prayer was used in the ancient world to be freed from fires (Dan 3), from beasts (Dan 6), and from famine (1 Kgs 18; Jas 5:17-18); and yet it had not received its form from Christ. How much greater, then, is the work of Christian prayer?!

Tertullian * These three youths became an example for all believers, for they did not fear the crowd of governors, nor were they terrified at hearing the king's words, nor did they shrink when they saw the flame of the furnace glowing, but counted all men and the whole world as nothing, keeping the fear of God alone before their eyes.

If Daniel stood far off in silence, yet he encouraged them to be joyful and good, and smiled at them. Indeed he himself rejoiced for the witness they bore, and for the understanding that had come to them as it had come to him, so that the three youths might receive the crown of victory over Satan.
* (The king) called the three youths by their names, but he did not find a name by which to call the fourth, for He had not yet (become incarnate) and become Jesus, born of the Virgin.
* They were honored not only by God but also by the king. They taught the foreign and alien nations to worship God.

St. Hippolytus of Rome * When the furnace was closed upon them, the flames fled, the blaze gave refreshment, and the Lord was present with them, affirming that no power stands against those who confess Him and His martyrs, for those who trust in God receive no harm, but are always safe from dangers.
* They added that God is able to do all things, but they did not speak thus in order to seek temporal deliverance, but to enjoy the glory of eternal freedom and eternal security.

* By saying "But if not..." they let the king know that they were also able to die for the God whom they worship. For this is the power of courage and faith. And with faith, knowing God's power to rescue from present death does not mean fear of death nor flight from it. By this faith is proved with greater power.

* The three youths Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were equal in age, united in love, steadfast in faith, persevering in virtue, stronger than the flame and the punishments laid upon them, declaring that they obey God alone, and know Him and worship Him alone.

St. Cyprian * The three holy youths showed themselves superior to the pleasures of lust, and despised the king's wrath, and were marked by courage without fear of the terrors of the furnace of fire that Nebuchadnezzar commanded to be kindled. They proved that the golden statue worshipped as a god is of no use...
* How did the three youths triumph over the power of fire? Was it not by perseverance?
St. Basil the Great * The three youths in Babylon became renowned through the flames.

St. Augustine The great men gathered, probably those who had complained against the youths, but before discussing the matter among themselves, perhaps to find what would justify their slander, the king issued his decree to destroy whoever stands against their God, offering them temporal honors as well. But he neither condemned idol worship nor abandoned it. He mixed his honoring of the living God with idol worship and its abominations. He did not care to ask about the One who was with the three youths in the furnace in order to be joined to Him and enjoy Him.

entries.section: 6. The Song of the Three Youths:

paragraphs.text: Then the three began with one mouth to praise God and glorify Him and bless Him in the furnace. We will speak about this wonderful song, which the Church uses daily, when we speak about the deuterocanonical books, if the Lord wills.
* God is in His place even now, He is in our midst, He who of old made the fire of the furnace in Babylon cold.

St. Basil the Great * The three youths were righteous; they cried to the Lord while in the furnace, and as they praised, the fire became cold. The flame could not come near to harm the innocent and upright youths, since they praised God, and He saved them from the flame.
* It is clear that He did not forsake the three youths who praised in the furnace; the flames could not touch them.
St. Augustine
Let me walk with You in the midst of the furnace!
* Let the fires be kindled, let the flame blaze, let the enemy roar, so long as You are within me I do not tremble!
Turn the flames into dew!
Instead of groaning, let my life turn into a hymn of praise!
Be revealed in my depths, and be glorified in my weakness, O God of the impossible!
Reveal Yourself for the salvation of every human soul, O Savior of the world!
Grant me the spirit of prayer with praise, that I may defy through You the fires of affliction, and even the fires of the devil and his evil works!
I no longer fear even sin, for You are the giver of victory over it!

1 "Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth; Peace be multiplied unto you. 2 I thought it good to shew the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me. 3 How great are his signs! and how mighty are his wonders! his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation."
"Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth;
Peace be multiplied unto you" [1].

St. Jerome says that Nebuchadnezzar's letter was recorded among the prophets, so that no one might afterward claim that the book was not Daniel's composition, meaning by this the pagan Porphyry who attacked the book.

Nebuchadnezzar presents to us a royal letter issued from the depths of his heart after passing through the divine discipline into which he fell because of his arrogance. He was not ashamed to address this letter to all peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth, in which he declares the following:

a. It was the ancient custom of great kings to count themselves kings over all the earth, although the Babylonian Empire did not reach Gaul and other lands. So it was with Rome during the Roman Empire, which was called the seat of the empire of the whole world, although the empire did not extend to the whole world at that time.

b. A testimony from experience of the personal relationship between God and him, for He wrought signs and wonders toward him. Though God humbled him with severe discipline, he deserved this discipline, which was profitable to him. He glorifies God by acknowledging God's care for him, and by acknowledging his sins and that he deserved the discipline.
"I thought it good to shew the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me" [2].

c. He bears witness to God's surpassing power: "How great are his signs! and how mighty are his wonders!" [3]. By His signs here he means what St. Jerome says: [By the mercies of God (the king) was restored to his throne, so he praised the King of heaven and glorified Him, on the ground that all His works are truth and His ways judgment, and He is able to abase those who walk in pride].
d. He bears witness to the eternal Kingdom of God and His dominion that does not pass away, whereas human kingdoms, however great, must collapse.
"His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation" [3].
Note that the introduction of the decree carries a theological, biblical, theocratic language (the rule of God), and some see that this reveals Daniel's influence on the king and on his language.

God spoke with the king whom He had set as head over all the earth at that time, and yet the king grew in arrogance and pride. He bore witness to God with his mouth, but his heart was haughty. His awareness of the one holy God was temporary, and with his confession of Him he did not withdraw from his worship of pagan gods and his mistaken beliefs.

entries.section: 2. The summoning of the wise men to interpret his dream:

paragraphs.text: "4 I Nebuchadnezzar was at rest in mine house, and flourishing in my palace: 5 I saw a dream which made me afraid, and the thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me. 6 Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known unto me the interpretation of the dream. 7 Then came in the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers: and I told the dream before them; but they did not make known unto me the interpretation thereof. 8 But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and before him I told the dream, saying,
I Nebuchadnezzar was at rest in mine house, and flourishing in my palace" [4].

Before Nebuchadnezzar recounts the judgments of God that came upon him because of his pride, he gave a just account of the warning that was directed to him [4], when he was at rest in his house and flourishing in his palace. Recently he had defeated Egypt, and so all his victories over Syria, Phoenicia, Judea, Egypt, and Arabia were completed, and the wars were finished for him in the 34th or 35th year of his reign (Ezek 29:17). These successive victories gave him an opportunity to exercise the haughtiness of his heart and his pride. He felt that there were no longer any clouds in the sky of his life, and that there was no arm able to resist him or stand before him. He thought that peace had come and security was sure.

Some translate the word "at rest (selueh)" as "abundance"; for when a man receives in overflowing measure he becomes like the horse which, when it eats more food than necessary, grows unruly, and its rider cannot control it and lead it, and the rider is exposed to falling from it. Therefore God often restrains our bellies and does not give us all that we desire, not because He wants to deprive us, but because He wants us to walk as is fitting for us, so that we do not harm ourselves or Him.
"I saw a dream which made me afraid, and the thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me.
Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known unto me the interpretation of the dream.

entries.section: 2. The summoning of the wise men to interpret his dream:

paragraphs.text: Then came in the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers: and I told the dream before them; but they did not make known unto me the interpretation thereof" [5-7].

Here the king distinguishes this dream from ordinary dreams that spring from his daily circumstances, for he felt that it was an extraordinary dream, carrying a message from the Most High, so he summoned the wise men to interpret the dream.

Daniel was in the royal palace, and the king knew him perfectly well, yet he ignored him in order to summon by royal command all the wise men of Babylon before him, the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers, setting Daniel apart from them, and when they failed to interpret his dream he resorted to Daniel. He sought the expertise of the magicians while realizing the power and truth of the divine interpretation granted to Daniel the man of God. Had he summoned Daniel it would have been quicker and better for him, but he did not do so. This is often our own conduct, for the prophetic word is in our hands, and divine knowledge is not far from us, and yet we seek human expertise and ignore what is in our hands freely! Let us seek the work of God, who is almighty, all-wise, and loving toward us, who dwells in us, and let us hold fast to His promises, which are not far from us, instead of resorting to what is outside us!

The king told the magicians the dream and yet they could not interpret it, they who had said with certainty before: "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will shew the interpretation of it" (Dan 2:4, 7). What Isaiah had prophesied before concerning the daughter of Babylon was fulfilled: "Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee" (Isa 47:13).

entries.section: 2. The summoning of the wise men to interpret his dream:

paragraphs.text: But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and before him I told the dream" [8].

When all human arms had failed, the king summoned the man of God, Daniel, and told the dream before him. He spoke with him as a pagan king who believes in many gods, but he believes of Daniel that "the spirit of the holy gods is in him" [8].

Perhaps the king did not summon Daniel, despite his confidence in his ability to interpret the dream and that no secret is hidden from him, because he realized that the dream carried discipline and humiliation for him to be accomplished by the hands of Daniel's God, so he did not resort to him except under the utmost necessity.

"9 O Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and the interpretation thereof. 10 Thus were the visions of mine head in my bed; I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great. 11 The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth: 12 The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it. 13 I saw in the visions of my head upon my bed, and, behold, a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven; 14 He cried aloud, and said thus, Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches: 15 Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth: 16 Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over him. 17 This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men. 18 This dream I king Nebuchadnezzar have seen. Now thou, O Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation thereof, forasmuch as all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known unto me the interpretation: but thou art able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in thee."

"O Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and the interpretation thereof" [9].

He called him by the name that he had imposed on him, "Belteshazzar," thinking that by this he was honoring him by ascribing him to his pagan god, whereas the name wounded Daniel's feelings and mind, for on the one hand it deprived him of what his parents had given him as a name connected with the name of the living God, and on the other hand it tied him to an idol in which he did not believe.

He also called him "master of the magicians," and this too added to the wounds of his soul, for he wanted to withdraw from the magicians who had deceived the world with their vain sorcery, and did not want to be a chief over them. At the same time he knows two things about him:

a. That the spirit of the holy gods is in him [8-9]; what he utters is not from human expertise and temporal wisdom, but from the work of the divine Spirit in him. The king realized that all human expertise and knowledge had failed, so he summoned Daniel, who alone had knowledge springing not from human abilities but from the Spirit of the holy God.
b. That no secret is hidden from him [9], which removes from the king his anxiety and the disturbance of his soul.
"Thus were the visions of mine head in my bed; I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great.
The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth:

The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it.
I saw in the visions of my head upon my bed, and, behold, a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven; he cried aloud, and said thus,
Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches:

Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth:
Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over him [10-16].
Nebuchadnezzar was a lover of the trees of Lebanon; he would go to enjoy them, and bring timber from them for building, so God likened him to the huge tree which he admires.

The prophets often refer to the great and the chiefs as trees, as in (Ezek 17:5-7; 31:3, etc.; Jer 22:15; Ps 1:3; 37:35). And the historian Herodotus (Herodotus 7:19) relates that Ahasuerus saw a dream that he was crowned with an olive tree whose branches filled the whole earth, but the crown withered from upon his head, and he realized that his reign would surely end.

God wants those in authority and the great, all leaders as well as kingdoms, to be like trees in which all find their nourishment, rest, and security, but men and kingdoms have misused authority, turning it from service into haughtiness with exploitation. For this reason these trees had to be uprooted so that the tree of the Cross might be planted, which brings love and surpassing peace and inward joy to every heart.

In this chapter God warns King Nebuchadnezzar, declaring to him in a dream that he will fall under severe discipline because of his arrogance. In this warning we sense God's tenderness in His dealings with man, even with the arrogant pagan king. On the one hand He reveals to him the discipline that will come upon him, that perhaps he might turn back from his evil and be spared it, and He gave him a respite of a whole year to examine himself, but instead of repenting he became haughty. On the other hand, even in the warning He likened him to a useful tree that offers shade to the beasts of the wilderness, food for man and beast, and a dwelling for the birds of heaven, and the tree is also marked by beauty.
* Such men are exalted, not by the greatness of their virtues, but by their pride, therefore they are cut down and perish.
St. Jerome The king related to Daniel the dream of the huge tree, which was marked by the following:

a. Standing in the midst of the earth, growing, and its height reaches to heaven [10-11]. In the midst of the earth, that is, at the center from which the Babylonian imperial authority radiates over all nations and peoples. Both Origen and St. Jerome see that Jerusalem is the center of the earth, as the city of God in which the temple was set up to bless humanity worshipping God. Some Babylonian rabbis (Rabbis) see that Babylon too is in the middle of the earth, as it is on the same line. But from the spiritual side, if Jerusalem represents the heavenly royal palace, then Babylon represents the royal palace of the Antichrist and all his kingdom. If Nebuchadnezzar represents a tree planted in Babylon, the haughty mother of harlots, the true believer represents a tree planted in Jerusalem, in the house of the Lord.
b. The sight thereof to the end of all the earth [11].
c. Beautiful in appearance [12], a reference to Nebuchadnezzar's concern for architectural constructions and the adorning of the capital.
d. Its fruit much, and in it meat for all [12], a reference to the wealth and mighty resources of Nebuchadnezzar.
e. A place of protection for others [12], protecting the birds among its branches and the beasts of the field in its shade.

This is what God offers to man, to make him a king who dwells in the world like a royal palace, wanting his soul to be always growing. While being on the earth it rises to heaven, that it may rest in the bosom of the Father, be glorified in the ends of the world, beautiful without blemish, satisfying all, widening to embrace others with love and so give security and peace to those who love it!
When Nebuchadnezzar fell into pride he deserved discipline, so God sent an angel, whom He called a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, to discipline.

The angel is called a watcher because he is a spirit without a body, who neither sleeps nor needs rest, so he is ever wakeful night and day. He is also called thus because he moves to carry out God's will for the edification of His people, as the Psalmist says: "Bless the LORD, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word" (Ps 103:20).

He is also called holy because he bears no human weakness. We, however, suffer from weakness, not only because of the sins we commit, but because of the corruption that crept into us from our first parents, which afflicts our body as well as our heart and mind.

However far a man may attain in sanctification, so long as he is still in the flesh he is not called "the watcher, the holy one," because through the need of nature he must sleep, and through the struggle he is exposed to weaknesses. By this we can distinguish between angels and men, as between striving believers and believers who have put off the body and passed from the world.

a. That what happens, even to the pagan king, is not by a human plan but by divine permission. For He sent His watching angel from heaven to carry out this plan. He spoke to him in the language of the Chaldeans, for they believed in heavenly beings who judge the works of men and have authority to decide their fate.

b. With the discipline there is mercy, for God commanded that the roots be left in the earth so that the tree might grow again through humility and repentance, so the tree is not uprooted entirely, and the discipline is for a set time, seven times [16]. "For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant" (Job 14:7-9). And though He permitted him to eat grass with the beasts of the field, He did not deprive him of enjoying the dew of heaven.

c. The command was given to the beasts that sheltered under the tree and the birds dwelling among its branches to flee, a sign that all the men of the state would forsake him. This is the fruit of sin, that man feels isolation. It is counted that all have forsaken him in moments of distress, even those whose friendship he had won by his lavish gifts.

d. It is clear from the dream that the tree symbolizes a particular person, for it personifies the tree, saying in [15-16]: "Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him"; it did not say of the tree "it" but "he."

What does he mean by the heart here? The understanding, the will, the feelings, and the inner soul as a whole. For though trees have no heart, the dream is symbolic. The command issued removed from the king, not only his empire, but also his human nature for a time, for he was not worthy to live as a man even in the lowest degrees of humanity.
e. No king arose in his place, but his son Evil-merodach carried out the work during this period until his father returned to his senses and his throne.
f. The purpose of the discipline is the benefit of many [17].
In this phrase [16] God assures the king that he will not be able to escape the discipline that He declares to him through the dream.

"This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men.
This dream I king Nebuchadnezzar have seen.
Now thou, O Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation thereof, forasmuch as all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known unto me the interpretation:
but thou art able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in thee" [17-18].

The word "word (pethegma)" here perhaps means a command or decree (edict), as in (Esth 1:20). So what was declared is a divine, heavenly decree. But why is the decree ascribed to the watching holy angels; is it a divine command or an angelic one?
Without doubt the command is divine, issued by God alone without any heavenly creature; as for ascribing it here to them, it is to affirm their positive role.

With the angels' perfect obedience to God, and their carrying out His commands, they pray for the salvation of the whole world. They ask that God intervene to discipline the proud who blaspheme against God, not to take vengeance on them, but to bring them back to the way of truth. It is as though what issued from God came in harmony with the desire of the heavenly ones' hearts, and their continual petitions, so that the command is counted as though it issued from them.

"19 Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him. The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee. Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies. 20 The tree that thou sawest, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached unto the heaven, and the sight thereof to all the earth; 21 Whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all; under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the fowls of the heaven had their habitation: 22 It is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth. 23 And whereas the king saw a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, and saying, Hew the tree down, and destroy it; yet leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven times pass over him; 24 This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree of the most High, which is come upon my lord the king: 25 That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. 26 And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule. 27 Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity."
"Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him.
The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee.
Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies" [19].

We should not wonder at Daniel's bewilderment and his grief over the disaster that was to befall the king of Babylon, for though the king was a tyrant and unjust, who took the Jewish people captive with other peoples, yet since Daniel worked in the palace he was bound to pray for him. God had commanded them by Jeremiah to pray for the prosperity of Babylon, for in this lay their peace (Jer 29:7). And because the seventy years had not yet been completed, it was not right for the believers to ask the king for a return, but they submitted to him in sincere obedience and served him faithfully without hatred. For this Daniel grieved when he learned what would befall the king.

"The tree that thou sawest, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached unto the heaven, and the sight thereof to all the earth; whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all; under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the fowls of the heaven had their habitation: it is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth" [20-22].

Here Daniel's marvelous wisdom appears, for with his love for the king and his humility before him, and his true longing to rescue him from the disaster, he spoke with him as a servant of the Word with all frankness, and uttered to him the divine truth. The prophet Daniel gives a practical lesson in service, for the servant is gentle with sinners and longs for their salvation, and if he rebukes he does not forget himself as a weak man; and at the same time he does not placate sinners at the expense of the truth, nor conceal God's wrath against sin. The prophet Daniel, who was gentle with the king, did not fear him, but with all boldness said to him: "It is thou, O king." He did not hesitate, nor offer excuses, nor speak in language that shows the slightest doubt, but with certainty declared to him that he is the tree upon which the disaster comes.

"And whereas the king saw a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, and saying, Hew the tree down, and destroy it; yet leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven times pass over him".

St. Jerome asks who will bind the king with a band of iron and brass, and answers: [It is very clear; all the insane are bound with chains to keep them from harming themselves or attacking others with weapons].
This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree of the most High, which is come upon my lord the king" [23-24].

While the prophet Daniel affirms that the dream, with all its bitterness, applies to the king, he addresses the king respectfully as "my lord the king." He presents the divine discipline without making light of the king or insulting him with a wounding word.

"That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will" [25].

Kings, especially those who are always victorious, often count themselves above every law; they command and are not commanded, they demand the obedience of others and it never crosses their heart to submit to others. They often forget their human nature, as though they were of a nature other than that of all other men. Now the prophet Daniel gives him the interpretation of the dream not to remind him that he is a man with human weakness, but that he will fall under discipline and so lose, together with the kingdom, his human nature, to become on the level of the beasts of the field. He will be cut off from among men to live as among a herd of oxen or swine.
"And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule" [26].

The prophet Daniel prepares Nebuchadnezzar for repentance, opening to him the door of hope, for with the discipline God's mercies are declared, which await his repentance to restore to him abundantly what he lost. For God disciplines not to humble man, but to lift him up and grant him the gift of knowledge, saying to him "after that thou shalt have known..." So discipline is a divine school for enjoying a surpassing heavenly knowledge.

"Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity" [27].

Daniel remained silent for a time, perplexed, so the king felt the gravity of the dream and encouraged him to speak, declaring to him that he would accept the matter whatever it was. Daniel was astonished and his thoughts troubled him for two reasons:
a. The fall of a great king like this to the lowest level, that he should have the heart of a beast of the wilderness.
b. That it was he who gives the interpretation to the king, and he wished the king well.
The king encouraged Daniel to speak, either from a desire to know the truth, or out of curiosity.
* He made the truth clear without insulting the king, so as to avoid appearing to accuse the king of sinful pride, but rather of great loftiness.

St. Jerome Daniel ended his speech by opening before the king the door of hope through repentance and works of mercy, leaving his sins. Daniel longed for Nebuchadnezzar's repentance so that he would not fall under this severe discipline, but that his enemies would fall into it. Therefore he gave him counsel to be gentle with the poor and needy. By this, as his heart turns from cruelty, violence, and selfishness to love and giving, he finds grace in the eyes of God.
* If you open your hands to the poor, Christ also opens His doors to you so that you may enter as into Paradise.

Father Caesarius * Let us say that Nebuchadnezzar performed works of mercy with the poor according to Daniel's counsel, therefore the sentence was postponed for twelve months. But when he was walking in his palace in Babylon and said arrogantly: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built?!"..., he therefore lost the virtue of giving by the evil of his pride.

* We also read in Jeremiah of God's instruction to the Jewish people that He obliges them to pray for the Babylonians, for the peace of the captives is bound up with the peace of those who took them captive.
St. Jerome

"28 All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar. 29 At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon. 30 The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty? 31 While the word was in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying, O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee. 32 And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. 33 The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws. 34 And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation: 35 And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou? 36 At the same time my reason returned unto me; and for the glory of my kingdom, mine honour and brightness returned unto me; and my counsellors and my lords sought unto me; and I was established in my kingdom, and excellent majesty was added unto me."
"All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar.
At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon.
The king spake, and said,
Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
While the word was in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying,

O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee. And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will" [28-32].
The Hebrew word mehelek indicates that the king was walking on the roof of the palace. The easterners practiced the custom of walking on the roof.
The king could see all of Babylon "from the roof," especially if the palace was built on a high hill.

In pride he thought he was a god, so he descended to become like a beast, as God said to Job: "behold every one that is proud, and abase him" (Job 10:11). He ascribed everything to himself, his power and his majesty, not to God, the giver of power and wisdom. He also ignored his predecessors who founded the city. But the wise Solomon, who built the temple, says: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain" (Ps 127:1).

"The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws.

And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation" [33-34].

In his pride he ascribed to himself Babylon with its walls, its public gardens, its temple of the god Bel, and the royal palace. Herodotus attributes Babylon to Semiramis and Nitocris, while Berosus and Abydenus relate that the Babylonians, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, added much to the old city, for Nebuchadnezzar built a splendid palace and the walls of the city. It may be gathered from Nitocris that Nebuchadnezzar's wife adorned the city.

Critics have attacked this text [30], saying that historically Nebuchadnezzar did not build Babylon, but in modern discoveries thousands of bricks were found in Babylon inscribed on the underside "Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabopolassar." Moreover, the word "build" here does not mean mere founding, but is also used for enlarging and adding. And let us not forget that many kings were accustomed to bury the glories of their predecessors and ascribe everything to themselves, by merely changing the form of the thing or adding to it.
* Had he not lifted his eyes toward heaven he would not have recovered his former mind.
Furthermore, by saying: "mine understanding returned unto me," he showed that he had not lost his outward appearance but only his mind.

St. Jerome By saying "from generation to generation" he does not mean only the generations to come, but, as St. Jerome says, that when his mind returned to him he perceived the mystery of the Kingdom of God, which passes from the Law to the Gospel.

"And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?" [35].

Tyrants often think that God is a prisoner of heaven, with no role in the affairs of men; and they do what they please like gods and there is none to resist them. Now the king sees that the God of heaven moves men, and leads and orders as He wills, and the earth is in the grasp of His hand just as heaven is!

At the same time my reason returned unto me; and for the glory of my kingdom, mine honour and brightness returned unto me; and my counsellors and my lords sought unto me; and I was established in my kingdom, and excellent majesty was added unto me [36].
Nebuchadnezzar did not repent although God left him twelve months, that is, a whole year after the dream. On the contrary, the king was struck with haughtiness and so the dream was fulfilled in him.

The dream was not fulfilled until after a year, God giving the king a long opportunity to examine himself and repent, to be gentle with the captives and care for the needy, but his pride only grew worse.

The king was struck with a state of madness that robbed him of his consciousness as a man; he became like the beasts of the wilderness, eating grass. Perhaps he was afflicted with lycanthropy, a disease in which the sufferer imagines that he has been transformed into a wolf.

* After that Babylonian king was stripped of the human form in his seven miserable years and became neglected because of his disobedience to the Lord, in bearing the bodily suffering he not only recovered his kingdom, but, what is more, accomplished the good pleasure of God...

Tertullian God, who moved Nebuchadnezzar to discipline His people for a time by their captivity, now declares to him that all things proceed with His permission. He permitted his men to drive him from rule and bind him because of his madness, and now He moves them to restore him to the kingship without their perceiving the hidden hand of God.
"Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase" [37].

When he completed the period of discipline his mind returned to him, so he lifted his gaze toward heaven as a repentant man seeking the mercies of God. His soul was crushed within him, and he glorified God. He realized that no man can reign forever, and that all kingdoms before God are as nothing. Or perhaps, when Nebuchadnezzar lifted his eyes to heaven glorifying God, God lifted the discipline from him.

Some thought that there is no evidence in history pointing to Nebuchadnezzar's madness, which makes the report historically untrue. In Berosus too, as appears in Josephus the Jewish historian, there is something that points to the reality of the king's madness. But it must be pointed out that even if external sources do not contain anything that indicates this madness of the king, this does not mean that the report is historically untrue.
"And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus" [21].
Tame my soul, for it has grown unruly!
* You gave me an abundance of good things and gifts, and I was filled and became sated, and my soul grew unruly.
Who can tame it but You, who care for my salvation?!
* Deprive me of some gifts, grant me humility before You, if there is edification in it for my depths!
But do not deprive me of Yourself, for You are the portion of my soul and my eternal inheritance!
* I have wronged Your love and the riches of Your gifts, for my soul grew unruly without restraint!
How hard it is for me to keep humility of mind amid the abundance of Your gifts!
Set my weakness before my eyes, that my mind may be humbled.
Take my hand, that I may walk with You in the way of Your love!
* Grant me, O Lord, the spirit of Daniel the prophet, the servant.
May I long for the salvation of sinners and be gentle with them, yet without flattery at the expense of the divine truth.
May I not fear a king however great his tyranny, nor hide Your word however stern it may seem!
* Your threats terrified Nebuchadnezzar; I find the sweetness of Your love amid Your threats to me.
Teach me to dedicate all my life to obeying You.
Your threats and Your promises are for the edification of my soul!
* My sin brought me down under divine discipline; it drove me, as it were, into the herd of oxen or swine.
Let me return to You, and You will carry me into the fellowship of the saints, and lift me up to the life of the heavenly ones.
And grant me a surpassing heavenly knowledge!

1 In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first. 2 And I saw in a vision; and it came to pass, when I saw, that I was at Shushan in the palace, which is in the province of Elam; and I saw in a vision, and I was by the river of Ulai.

This vision took place a short time before the fall of Babylon, for the prophet Daniel saw himself as one who was in Shushan, the capital of the province of Elam, west of Persia, east of Babylon and south of Media.
"In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first" [1].

Daniel was granted by the Lord to stand as in a high watchtower, to see the distant things that no one else sees, which some may think illogical, and sometimes even impossible. This gift is offered to the faithful soul that throws itself into the bosom of God, who lifts it up as on the wings of a dove, to see even what lies beyond time.

This vision was granted to him two years after the previous vision, and shortly before the fall of Babylon (Dan 5). For this reason the vision passed over the Babylonian Empire and revealed the kingdom of Media and Persia (the ram), which is attacked by the kingdom of the Macedonians (the he-goat).
"And I saw in a vision; and it came to pass, when I saw, that I was at Shushan in the palace, which is in the province of Elam; and I saw in a vision, and I was by the river of Ulai" [2].

The city of Shushan, or Susa, is described in the Holy Bible as the citadel. It held a special position, since it was the capital of Persia; later, in the days of the Persian Empire, it came to share the status of capital with Babylon. It lies about 250 miles east of Babylon; one of them was used in winter and the other in summer, and it became the capital of Cyrus. Daniel was in the palace in Babylon, but in the vision he saw himself as though he were by the river of Ulai.
