Some thought that Daniel was in the city of Shushan, but this is not acceptable, for it was not possible for Daniel the captive to leave Babylon and dwell in Shushan, which belonged to Persia; rather he saw himself thus in the vision. Perhaps God permitted this to reassure him that, as he had served his people during the Babylonian rule, he would serve them also during the Persian rule. Most probably the palace of Shushan had not yet been built, because the Persian Empire had not yet flourished.

3 Then I lifted up mine eyes, and saw, and, behold, there stood before the river a ram which had two horns: and the two horns were high; but one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last. 4 I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; so that no beasts might stand before him, neither was there any that could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and became great.
In the previous vision Daniel saw four beasts, but here he sees two animals, the first being a ram with two horns.

As the time of Babylon's collapse before Persia and Media drew near, Daniel saw this vision. He saw a ram standing by the river, having two high horns, one higher than the other. St. Hippolytus of Rome says: [By this ram, pushing westward, northward and southward, he means Darius, king of the Persians, who overcame all the nations, as it is said, "no beasts might stand before him".]
"Then I lifted up mine eyes, and saw, and, behold, there stood before the river a ram which had two horns: and the two horns were high; but one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last.

I saw the ram pushing westward, and northward, and southward; so that no beasts might stand before him, neither was there any that could deliver out of his hand; but he did according to his will, and became great" [3-4].

When the prophet Daniel felt that he was called to see divine mysteries of the future, he lifted up his eyes to see. It is as though the vision, although it appears to concern the emergence of the kingdoms of Persia, Media and Greece, in its essence touches the eternity of the believers and their enjoyment of what is above time. Thus it is not for us to ignore chronological history, but when the Spirit of God lifts up our eyes we see God's hidden plan, which works through history to carry us beyond history.

With wonderful precision the kingdom of Persia was likened to the ram with two horns, one higher than the other, because Persia became greater than Media. Cyrus the Persian married the daughter of his maternal uncle Cyaxares (Darius the Mede). Darius was very weak in character compared with Cyrus, who far surpassed his father-in-law; nevertheless he left him as a partner with him in the rule, and so the prophecy was fulfilled literally.

Here the two horns correspond to the two sides of the second beast (the bear) in the previous vision, where it raised itself up on one side (Dan 7:5), and also to the two shoulders of the great metal image, the Colossus, in Nebuchadnezzar's dream mentioned in the second chapter. The pushing of the ram signifies the swift victories achieved by the Persians.
Since Persia was likened to the ram, the other kings were likened to the beasts, which could not stand before him, nor escape from his hands.
Marcellinus says: [When the king of the Persians was at the head of his army, he wore the head of a ram on his head instead of the crown.]

5 And as I was considering, behold, an he goat came from the west on the face of the whole earth, and touched not the ground: and the goat had a notable horn between his eyes. 6 And he came to the ram that had two horns, which I had seen standing before the river, and ran unto him in the fury of his power. 7 And I saw him come close unto the ram, and he was moved with choler against him, and smote the ram, and brake his two horns: and there was no power in the ram to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground, and stamped upon him: and there was none that could deliver the ram out of his hand. 8 Therefore the he goat waxed very great: and when he was strong, the great horn was broken; and for it came up four notable ones toward the four winds of heaven.
"And as I was considering, behold, an he goat came from the west on the face of the whole earth, and touched not the ground: and the goat had a notable horn between his eyes.
And he came to the ram that had two horns, which I had seen standing before the river, and ran unto him in the fury of his power" [5-6].

When the ram appeared with power and authority, pushing every beast it met, an enemy appeared to it: a he-goat with a notable horn between his eyes. The prophet saw him coming from the west, where Greece lies, west of Persia. The goat was so swift that his feet did not touch the ground [5]. With his army he was more like a bird flying in the air than one coming over land or by the fleet at sea. Persia was likened to the ram in comparison with the Greek kingdom, which was likened to the he-goat. For the goat is more agile and swifter in movement than the ram. So Alexander the Great was swifter in his movements.
He smote the ram, and brake his two horns, and cast him down to the ground, and stamped upon him, and there was none that could deliver the ram out of his hand [7].

"And I saw him come close unto the ram, and he was moved with choler against him, and smote the ram, and brake his two horns: and there was no power in the ram to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground, and stamped upon him: and there was none that could deliver the ram out of his hand" [7].

This is a true vision that was fulfilled more than 200 years later. Here God shows His prophet the victory of Alexander, who subdued the whole East, entering into many battles; but the vision focuses on Persia, which dominated many nations, and which was previously likened to the ram that pushes in every direction of the world.

He saw the goat come to the ram, a thing that no one expected, since the great cities were fortified, and the distance between Persia and Greece was great. But Alexander reached Persia and defeated it with unexpected power and speed. Darius was defeated in two dramatic battles. He was defeated in the first battle and tried to gather his forces again, and indeed he entered with him into a second battle, but his followers betrayed him, and the battle ended with his being killed by them.

Some historians say that Alexander claimed to be the son of the god Jupiter Ammon, who was symbolized in the form of a goat, and historical pictures have been discovered depicting a goat with a single horn as a symbol of the ancient Greek armies.
"Therefore the he goat waxed very great: and when he was strong, the great horn was broken; and for it came up four notable ones toward the four winds of heaven" [8].

St. Hippolytus of Rome says: [By the he-goat coming from the west he means Alexander the Macedonian, coming from Greece... Alexander stirred up war against Darius and overcame him, and established himself as lord over the whole kingdom after he had defeated him with a shameful defeat and destroyed his camp. After the goat was glorified, his great horn was broken, and four horns came up under it toward the four winds of heaven. For when Alexander had established himself as lord over all the land of the Persians and subdued its people, he died, and his kingdom was divided among four rulers.]

The goat waxed very great, and at the height of his greatness a wonderful change occurred: the notable horn was broken, and in its place came up four notable ones, extending toward the four winds of heaven [8]. At the death of Alexander the Great, his kingdom was divided among his four generals into four kingdoms: Macedonia, Thrace, Syria and Egypt. None of them was equal to him in strength. Historians differ concerning his death; some think he died of sickness, and others think he died poisoned. Before his death he was asked who should succeed him; in his pride he saw no one worthy to succeed him, and he said: "The man who counts himself most worthy of this empire!" He had two sons, one of them by Roxana, the daughter of Darius, and he also had a brother called Aridaeus, but he saw none of them worthy to succeed him, as though there were no one in the whole world like him. When he became unable to speak, he took the ring from his hand and gave it to Perdiccas. After his death there were many disturbances and about 15 generals were killed.

Cassander, the son of Antipater, became king over Macedonia after killing Olympias, the mother of Alexander, and his sister, his son, his wife Roxana, and many of his relatives. The generals lost confidence in one another, and each general feared his colleagues, for a spirit of treachery and betrayal prevailed among them. Finally, 15 years after his death, the kingdom was divided into four parts, which are:
A. Macedonia, over which Cassander the son of Antipater reigned, and to which were joined some parts of Thrace together with the cities of Greece.
B. Syria, Babylonia and all the kingdoms of the East, over which Seleucus Nicanor reigned.
C. Asia Minor, over which Antigonus reigned, annexing Phrygia, Paphlagonia and the other Asian regions, after killing 5 or 6 of the generals.
D. Egypt, over which Ptolemy the son of Lagos reigned.
These are the four notable horns [8] that ruled the world in the East, the West, the North and the South.

9 And out of one of them came forth a little horn, which waxed exceeding great, toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the pleasant land. 10 And it waxed great, even to the host of heaven; and it cast down some of the host and of the stars to the ground, and stamped upon them. 11 Yea, he magnified himself even to the prince of the host, and by him the daily sacrifice was taken away, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down. 12 And an host was given him against the daily sacrifice by reason of transgression, and it cast down the truth to the ground; and it practised, and prospered. 13 Then I heard one saint speaking, and another saint said unto that certain saint which spake,

"How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice, and the transgression of desolation, to give both the sanctuary and the host to be trodden under foot?" 14 And he said unto me, "Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed." [9-14].

What is this little horn but the antichrist of the Old Testament, Antiochus Epiphanes, who also symbolizes the Antichrist at the end of the ages? He was called the little horn, not by comparison with the rest of the kings of his time, but because no one expected him to take the throne after his father; yet he seized the rule by his cunning and craftiness. Epiphanes reigned over Syria (the northern kingdom of the Greek Empire) about the year 175 BC. The prophet Daniel spoke of him in more detail in (Dan 11:21-35). He was called the most defiled man of the Old Testament, and he persecuted the Jews. After the death of his brother he met the people and pretended great kindness and deceived them, so they made him king; and he slaughtered a swine and sprinkled its blood on the altar and the holy vessels, and forbade the offering of the daily sacrifices [11], on pain of death.

* Antiochus, called Epiphanes, arose from the line of Alexander, and when he reigned over Syria and subdued Egypt under his authority, he went up to Jerusalem, entered the Temple, and seized all the treasures of the house of the Lord, the golden lampstand, the table and the altar, and made a great slaughter in the land, as it is written: "The sanctuary shall be trodden under foot for one thousand three hundred evenings and mornings." It came to pass that the sanctuary remained desolate all this time - three and a half years - so the one thousand three hundred days were fulfilled. Then Judas Maccabeus appeared after the death of his father Mattathias and resisted him, and destroyed the camp of Antiochus, and delivered the city, and cleansed the sanctuary and restored it carefully, as ordained in the Law.
This was clearly described in the books of the Maccabees.

St. Hippolytus of Rome: "Waxed great toward the south" [9], that is, toward Egypt, for he wanted to seize Egypt, but the Senate sent Pompilius to him to make him leave Egypt, and in his deceitful way he asked the messenger for a delay in order to leave Egypt; but the messenger, holding a staff, drew a circle on the ground around him and said: "Before you go out of this circle, give me an answer, and do not deceive me by saying that you are seeking the counsel of advisers." So he was compelled to leave Egypt. But afterwards he entered into war against Ptolemy Philopator, king of Egypt.
He turned toward the east [9], for his kingdom extended as far as Ptolemais, and he fought those who rebelled against him in Persia.

Then toward "the pleasant land" [9], that is, the glorious lands, or the land of promise, "Canaan". As it is said in Jeremiah, "And give thee a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the hosts of nations" (Jer 3:19); "And hast given them this land, which thou didst swear to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey" (Jer 31:22). It was also called the pleasant land because of the presence of the glorious Temple of the Lord in Judah, and Antiochus fought the Jews and defiled their Temple.

Antiochus (or the Antichrist) waxes great even to the host of heaven and casts down some of the host and of the stars to the ground [10]. Thus God declares to His prophet Daniel concerning His Church that she is heaven, and that the believers are the host of Christ and her stars.

And as Antiochus opposed the believers - the Church of the Old Testament - and killed many, so the Antichrist will exert all his effort to destroy the stars of the New Testament. For this reason the Lord Christ says concerning His final coming: "When the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" As He also says concerning the Antichrist: "if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect."

The matter does not stop at the stars of heaven or its host, but the enemy magnifies himself against the prince of the host [11], that is, the Jewish high priest whom Antiochus Epiphanes persecuted. St. Jerome thinks that by the prince of the host he means God Himself, the Lord of hosts, for Antiochus stood against Him, and did not leave any part of the Temple holy for the worship of the living God, but defiled the whole Temple and its annexes. And since he forbade the offering of the daily sacrifice endelekhismos, the temple of the Lord became as though it did not exist. St. Jerome says that Antiochus did this not because of his courage but because of the sins of the people. All this bears a symbol of what the Antichrist, who sets himself up as God, will do.

And the matter does not stop at opposing the worship of God, but extends to corrupting the divine teachings, for it says of him that "it cast down the truth to the ground" [12]. Thus the vision links worship with sound doctrine. On the other hand, the enemy of good can cast down the truth to the ground, but he cannot snatch it away from heaven. It is as though whoever lives in the heavenly realms carries within him, alongside spiritual worship, the truth itself.

When Daniel's heart was lifted up to heaven, he saw an angel (a saint) asking another angel, although some think that he was asking the Word of God: "How long shall be the vision concerning the daily sacrifice...?" The angels do not know all the mysteries (Eph 3:10), but in their love for mankind and their longing for the perfection of their glory they inquire about what concerns the Church, and perhaps they feared that the period of tribulation would be prolonged, so that the believers would lose their faith and their crowns.

entries.section: Scholars differed concerning this little horn:

paragraphs.text: A. Some think that it is the very same little horn mentioned in chapter 7.

B. Others distinguish between the two, holding that the little horn mentioned in chapter 7 refers to the Antichrist, while the one mentioned here refers to Antiochus Epiphanes, whom some regard as the "antichrist" of the Old Testament period.

C. There is an opinion that reconciles the two previous opinions, namely that what is mentioned here in chapter eight refers to Antiochus, who in turn refers to the Antichrist; as though what is mentioned in chapter seven refers to the Antichrist directly, while this chapter refers to him indirectly.

As for the period concerning the vindication or cleansing of the sanctuary, which is 2300 evenings and mornings: lest the day here be understood as a symbol of a year, it says "evenings and mornings", which means 2300 real days. St. Jerome thinks that it equals 6 years and three months, and that it represents the period from the beginning of Antiochus' opposition to worship until Judas Maccabeus triumphed over him. St. Hippolytus of Rome, on the other hand, thinks that 2300 evenings and mornings means 1150 days (2300÷2), since the two daily sacrifices (the morning and the evening) were forbidden during the persecution, and this equals about three and a half years, for Judas Maccabeus cleansed the Temple after it had been defiled by Antiochus.

Many commentators think that 2300 evenings and mornings affirms that they are real days, and that they equal 6 years, 4 months and 20 prophetic days, since the year in the Holy Bible equals 360 prophetic days and the month 30 days. This is the actual period that begins on 5 August 71 BC, that is, from the beginning of the transgression of desolation, when Jason was appointed high priest through intrigues, and pledged to the king that he would pay him 260 talents of silver if he would permit him to establish a place to teach the young men of the Jews the customs of the pagans and to call them Antiochenes, and he permitted him to do so. And indeed he introduced the customs of the pagans among his people, and they adopted their dress and wore their hats, and the priests despised the Temple of God and its sacrifices and were busy with the Greek games, preferring them above everything. As it is said in the book of the Maccabees: "In those days there went out of Israel wicked men, and persuaded many, saying: Let us go and make a covenant with the nations that are round about us: for since we departed from them we have found much evil; and the saying seemed good in their eyes... and they forsook the holy covenant, and joined themselves to the nations, and were sold to do mischief" (1 Macc 1:11-15). If Daniel's prophecy is reckoned from this event until the restoration of worship to its origin and the cleansing of the sanctuary on 25 December 165, the period is exactly 2300 days. In other words, what is mentioned here includes the period in which all the calamities befell the Temple in the days of Antiochus Epiphanes, from the first transgression of desolation to the end of the period of the abolition of the daily sacrifice, when Judas Maccabeus delivered the Jews from Antiochus.
The painful events that Jerusalem suffered at that time are:
A. The appointment of Jason as high priest and his sharing with Antiochus in the pagan abominations.
B. The attack of Antiochus on Jerusalem, his entering the Temple and plundering its treasures, and the offering of a swine on the altar (1 Kgs 1:20-28).

C. Two years later, when the false report of his death spread and the Jews rejoiced, he sent to them Apollonius, one of his commanders, who dealt cruelly with the city, then burned it, razed its walls, and built from its ruins a strong fortress on a mountain overlooking the Temple (1 Macc 2:29; 2 Macc 5:11-14).
D. He officially forbade the offering of burnt offerings and sacrifices in the Temple (1 Macc 1:54), and that was in the month of June 197 BC.
Concerning what befell the Jews at the hands of Antiochus Epiphanes, we distinguish two main periods:
A. A period of 2300 days that includes all the previous events, beginning with Jason's appointment as high priest and ending with the victory of Judas Maccabeus.

B. A period of 1290 days, or about three and a half years, beginning with the removal of the daily sacrifice, the setting up of the statue of Jupiter in the Temple, and the defiling of the sanctuary after Antiochus took possession of Jerusalem by means of his commander Apollonius.

15 And it came to pass, when I, even I Daniel, had seen the vision, and sought for the meaning, then, behold, there stood before me as the appearance of a man. 16 And I heard a man's voice between the banks of Ulai, which called, and said, "Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision." 17 So he came near where I stood: and when he came, I was afraid, and fell upon my face: but he said unto me, "Understand, O son of man: for at the time of the end shall be the vision." 18 Now as he was speaking with me, I was in a deep sleep on my face toward the ground: but he touched me, and set me upright. 19 And he said, "Behold, I will make thee know what shall be in the last end of the indignation: for at the time appointed the end shall be. 20 The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia. 21 And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king. 22 Now that being broken, whereas four stood up for it, four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not in his power. 23 And in the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors are come to the full, a king of fierce countenance, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up. 24 And his power shall be mighty, but not by his own power: and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people. 25 And through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and by peace shall destroy many: he shall also stand up against the Prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand. 26 And the vision of the evening and the morning which was told is true: wherefore shut thou up the vision; for it shall be for many days." 27 And I Daniel fainted, and was sick certain days; afterward I rose up, and did the king's business; and I was astonished at the vision, but none understood it.
"And it came to pass, when I, even I Daniel, had seen the vision, and sought for the meaning, then, behold, there stood before me as the appearance of a man.
And I heard a man's voice between the banks of Ulai, which called, and said,
Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision" [15-16].

The prophet Daniel desired a fuller interpretation of the vision, for he knew little; but for his own benefit and for the benefit of the Church as a whole he desired to search for the meaning, and before he asked he saw "the appearance of a man" [15]; most probably the Word of God before the Incarnation, who has authority to command the archangel Gabriel to interpret the vision for him [16]. It is as though God, who knows the secrets of the heart, when He sees the inner man longing for the truth, grants it to him in abundance, and asks His heavenly servants to reveal to him some of the hidden mysteries.
"So he came near where I stood: and when he came, I was afraid, and fell upon my face:
but he said unto me, Understand, O son of man:
for at the time of the end shall be the vision.
Now as he was speaking with me, I was prostrate (in a deep sleep) on my face toward the ground: but he touched me, and set me upright.
And he said, Behold, I will make thee know what shall be in the last end of the indignation:
for at the time appointed the end shall be" [17-19].

St. Jerome justifies the calling of Daniel "son of man" by saying: [Since Ezekiel, Daniel and Zechariah saw that they were often in the company of angels, they were always reminded of their weakness, lest they be lifted up with pride and think that they shared in the nature or dignity of the angels. Therefore they were called sons of men (sons of Adam), that they might realize that they were nothing but human beings.]

When the archangel drew near to Daniel, the prophet fell in terror. Perhaps Daniel discovered the gravity of the vision, and God's concern to reveal its mysteries to him by means of an archangel, so he received this interpretation in fear and reverence. He recorded this for us so that we should not make light of the vision or treat its interpretation with contempt, but that our minds, like our lives, must be prepared to know it with diligence and seriousness. The angel made clear to him that this vision is "at the time of the end" [17], that is, it concerns the future. Here perhaps he means its fulfillment in the days of Antiochus and, even more, shortly before the last coming of Christ. He affirms that the vision will surely and fully be fulfilled, but at the appropriate time appointed for it.

The archangel raised him from his deep sleep, that his mind might be kindled with knowledge, and he comforted him, and also assured him of the destruction of this little horn. It is said that Antiochus died an evil death, as worms ate his body, like Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12). So also the Antichrist will be struck, and his kingdom will perish.
"The ram which thou sawest having two horns are the kings of Media and Persia.
And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
Now that being broken, whereas four stood up for it, four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not in his power.
And in the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors are come to the full, a king of fierce countenance, and understanding dark sentences, shall stand up.
And his power shall be mighty, but not by his own power:
and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practise, and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people.

And through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and by peace shall destroy many: he shall also stand up against the Prince of princes; but he shall be broken without hand" [22-25].

We have already explained what is stated in the previous phrases. Here the archangel affirms to Daniel the meaning of the ram and the he-goat, removing the least doubt concerning their interpretation.

Here he calls Antiochus a king of fierce countenance, that is, a king with a hard, unyielding face, and he also calls him one who understands dark sentences or riddles, because he was skilled in deception.

The prophet Daniel prophesied concerning Antiochus, saying that by peace or security he shall destroy many [25], and this was fulfilled when he sent his commander with 22,000 men to Jerusalem as a mission of peace. These soldiers would go in and out until the Jews felt secure with them, and the men treated the people with great kindness, so that they did not suspect them. And on the Sabbath, while the Jews were worshiping in the Temple, orders were given to kill them all, and thousands were killed, and thus by security he destroyed many.

The prophet Daniel also prophesied his standing up against the Prince of princes and his being broken without human hand [25], and this was accomplished when Antiochus Epiphanes opposed God Himself, the Prince of princes and King of kings. And he remained so for more than 6 years (2300 days). The Maccabees resisted him, and by their hands the Temple was cleansed and victory over him was achieved. He heard that the Jews under the leadership of the Maccabees had removed the statue of Jupiter Olympius from the Temple, which he himself had placed there, so he was greatly enraged and gathered a huge army and decided to exterminate the Jewish race completely, but he was struck with a very sharp pain in his bowels, and died at once from the intensity of the pain, and thus he perished by divine permission without the use of a human hand.
"And the vision of the evening and the morning which was told is true:
wherefore shut thou up (seal) the vision; for it shall be for many days.
And I Daniel fainted, and was sick certain days; afterward I rose up, and did the king's business;
and I was astonished at the vision, but none understood it" [26-27].

By saying: "the vision of the evening and the morning which was told is true" [26], he means that the vision is true in its dark aspect, where there is severe tribulation, and its bright aspect, where God declares the victory of His people.

Daniel could not bear the vision, so he became sick, unable to leave his bed, for some days. But he was terrified of what would befall the Church, whether in the days of Antiochus or of the Antichrist. Yet, as St. Jerome says: [He rose up to do the king's business, rendering unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's (Lk 20:25).

In any case Daniel did not grasp all the mysteries of the vision, and the future unsealing of them with the passing of the times, for he says: "I was astonished at the vision, but none understood it" [27].

entries.section: I became perplexed and did not understand!

paragraphs.text: * The archangel Gabriel accompanied Your prophet Daniel and gave him an interpretation of some of Your mysteries, and here he cries out after his body was loosed in weakness:
I was astonished at the vision, and did not understand!
* Reveal to me the mysteries of Your love, that I may see all history in the grasp of Your hands, and see my whole life as the object of Your care!
Grant me the company of Your angels, but remind me of my weakness lest I exalt myself.
Remember that I am a weak son of Adam.
In You I become strong and wise!
* Let the powerful kingdoms succeed one another, and let the Antichrist appear, for You alone are the fortress of the Church and her strength!
You will not allow him to reign except for a limited time!
His kingdom will end, and Your saints will reign in heaven forever!

entries.section: 1. Daniel the student of the prophecies:

paragraphs.text: 1 In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans; 2 In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem.
"In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans" [1].

The events of this chapter took place after the fall of Babylon, in the first year of the reign of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, or Astyages as the historian Xenophon calls him, that is, at approximately the same date as that of the sixth chapter, about the year 537 BC, a year before Cyrus allowed the Jews to return to Jerusalem. The name Ahasuerus was common among many of the kings of the kingdom of Persia and Media.

By the words "which was made king" it means that Darius did not become king by his own valor, but the kingship was given to him by another; that is, by Cyrus, the son of his sister and the husband of his daughter.

entries.section: 1. Daniel the student of the prophecies:

paragraphs.text: "In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem" [2].

Daniel appears not only as a prophet but also as a student of the prophecies (Jer 25:9-11; 29:10; 31:38; 2 Chr 36:21). He studies the word of God and the prophecies, and mixes his study with prayer, offering three prayers every day. His study was not to satisfy an intellectual pleasure, or out of curiosity to learn something new, but to enjoy the promises of God. Daniel had grown old and been retired; he had spent about 69 years in captivity, from 606 BC to 537 BC (until the moments of this vision); yet his heart never grew old, nor did he withdraw from the divine work as a man of God, but with time his soul was filled with strength and hope in God's true promises. For this reason Daniel took refuge in the Holy Bible, finding in it the treasure of these promises to which he clings. He also mixed his study of the Scripture with a life of asceticism and prayer in a spirit of contrition before God.

"I Daniel understood by books" [2]. Some liberal critics claim that the word "books" came in the definite form in the Hebrew language, and this means that the prophet Daniel was speaking of a complete canon of the books of the Old Testament, whereas they claim that this canon was not completed until the second century BC. What the critics claim is built on the ideas of the past three centuries, and scientific studies and research have proved the falsity of these claims:

First: The prophets did not write their books in order to hide them until someone came to place them in the canon, as the critics imagine; rather the people kept in memory what was in the books of the prophets before they were written, because the declarations in them were first proclaimed to the people and then recorded in books by the Holy Spirit afterward.

Second: These books were collected in the Temple and with individuals, especially the prophets and the scholars of religion. Naturally, everything written before Daniel was available to him in a copy. The original copy was always placed in the Temple, and many copies were also found in the synagogues that were established in the captivity for Jewish worship and as a temporary substitute for the Temple.

3 And I set my face unto the Lord God, to seek by prayer and supplications, with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes: 4 And I prayed unto the LORD my God, and made my confession, and said, "O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments; 5 We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments: 6 Neither have we hearkened unto thy servants the prophets, which spake in thy name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land. 7 O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and unto all Israel, that are near, and that are far off, through all the countries whither thou hast driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against thee. 8 O Lord, to us belongeth confusion of face, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against thee. 9 To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses, though we have rebelled against him; 10 Neither have we obeyed the voice of the LORD our God, to walk in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets. 11 Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law, even by departing, that they might not obey thy voice; therefore the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him. 12 And he hath confirmed his words, which he spake against us, and against our judges that judged us, by bringing upon us a great evil: for under the whole heaven hath not been done as hath been done upon Jerusalem. 13 As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil is come upon us: yet made we not our prayer before the LORD our God, that we might turn from our iniquities, and understand thy truth. 14 Therefore hath the LORD watched upon the evil, and brought it upon us: for the LORD our God is righteous in all his works which he doeth: for we obeyed not his voice. 15 And now, O Lord our God, that hast brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and hast gotten thee renown, as at this day; we have sinned, we have done wickedly. 16 O Lord, according to all thy mercy, turn away thine anger and thy fury from thy city Jerusalem, thy holy mountain: because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and thy people are become a reproach to all that are about us. 17 Now therefore, O our God, hear the prayer of thy servant, and his supplications, and cause thy face to shine upon thy sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord's sake. 18 O my God, incline thine ear, and hear; open thine eyes, and behold our desolations, and the city which is called by thy name: for we do not present our supplications before thee for our righteousnesses, but for thy great mercies. 19 O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God: for thy city and thy people are called by thy name."

When Daniel opened the Holy Bible and discovered the treasures of the heavenly promises, he realized that enjoying these treasures requires prayer mixed with fasting, together with humility and contrition. This book has revealed in more than one place the character of Daniel as a man of prayer. In his prayer here we notice the following:

entries.section: A. Prayer as a living encounter with God:

paragraphs.text: Knowing that neither he nor his people were spiritually prepared for the fulfillment of what God had promised, he took refuge in God, confessing his sins as he confesses the righteousness of God [3-14]. By this Daniel acknowledges that he awaits the divine work not on account of any merit of his own or of the people, that is, not on account of human righteousness [18].
"And I set my face unto the Lord God, to seek by prayer and supplications, with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes" [3].

Prayer for Daniel is not a routine act or a duty to which he is bound, but the enjoyment of beholding the face of God with the eyes of the heart, for he says: "I set my face unto God", so as to enter into a dialogue with Him in a spirit of love and humility. By this he fulfilled what the wise Solomon said on the day of the dedication of the house of the Lord: "If they sin against thee, (for there is no man that sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them, and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captives unto the land of the enemy, far or near; yet if they shall bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent, and make supplication unto thee in the land of them that carried them captives, saying, We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness; and so return unto thee with all their heart, and with all their soul, in the land of their enemies, which led them away captive, and pray unto thee toward their land, which thou gavest unto their fathers, the city which thou hast chosen, and the house which I have built for thy name: then hear thou in heaven..." (1 Kgs 8:46-48).

entries.section: B. Daniel did not lack faith that God fulfills His promises:

paragraphs.text: * Daniel asked God in sackcloth and ashes to fulfill His promise, not because Daniel lacked faith concerning what would happen in the future, but rather because he wanted to avoid the danger of the feeling of security that breeds indifference, and indifference breeds disobedience to God.
St. Jerome

entries.section: C. The sense of a personal relationship with God:

paragraphs.text: He calls: "the LORD my God" [4, 20]. Although he confesses his sins and those of his people, he approaches God not in dread, but in confidence and assurance in God as his personal friend, to whom he belongs, the giver of true promises.
"And I prayed unto the LORD my God, and made my confession, and said,
O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments" [4].
* "And I prayed unto Thee... O Lord, the great and dreadful God", meaning: You are fearful to those who despise Your commandments.
St. Jerome

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: He does not cast the blame on them alone, but on himself with them. The prophet Daniel offers us the substance of his prayer and confession, mixing the two, for he confesses in humility the greatness of the dreadful God and His mercies, as he confesses his own sins and those of his people. He begins his prayer by confessing the glory of God and His surpassing care for His people.

Daniel knew that God fulfills His promises to those who keep His commandments. The Holy Bible also links the divine covenant with the divine mercies, for He established the covenant relying upon His mercies. Through all ages the believer feels that God is faithful in His promises, true and merciful, yet it is fitting for the believer to prepare himself to enjoy the divine promises and mercies, by declaring his faith and his trust in God together with repentance from his sins. The Apostle says: "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord" (1 Cor 1:9); "but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able" (1 Cor 10:13); "But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil" (2 Thess 3:3).
"We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments" [5].

As the prophet continues to confess his sins, he declares that what befell him and his people came only because of their sins, for the captivity is a just discipline on account of disobedience. They have no right to complain of the brutality of the enemy who took them captive, or of the material harm, disgrace and shame that came upon them. He also often attributes the sins of the people to himself, and as St. Jerome says: [He looked upon the sins of the people as though he himself had committed them personally, on the basis that he was one of them, as we likewise read of the Apostle in the Epistle to the Romans.]

When we draw near to God in prayer with confession, we do not think that we obtain anything by our prayers, but as offenders against Him we appease Him by our faith in His love, His mercies and His righteousness.
The prophet Daniel used more than one expression in his confession of sins, among them:

We have sinned chetanu, which is perhaps related to the word "Satan", because the nature of Satan after his fall is to sin against God. And when we sin, we reject the Fatherhood of God, to declare sonship to Satan. As the Lord Christ said to the sinning Jews: "Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do" (Jn 8:44).
We have committed iniquity, that is, we have done iniquity or injustice.
We have done wickedly: our conduct has become unseemly.

We have rebelled reshegn, and rebellion is worse than sin, because in it there is a defiance of God's commandment and judgments. In rebellion there is a rejection of the divine light offered to us, as the Psalmist says: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path" (Ps 119:105), and an acceptance of darkness knowingly and willingly, and not out of weakness or ignorance.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: Neither have we hearkened unto thy servants the prophets, which spake in thy name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land" [6].

The prophet did not offer any justification for the error, but on the contrary justifies the discipline of God, who had warned them through His prophets. All shared in the error, whether at the level of the civil or religious leaders or at the level of the people, for all rushed toward evil collectively.
"O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee,
but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day;

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and unto all Israel, that are near, and that are far off, through all the countries whither thou hast driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against thee" [7].

If they have fallen under the divine wrath, in His wrath He is righteous, while confusion of faces is fitting for them, that is, falling on their faces before Him, confessing their error. As the Apostle says: "Let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged" (Rom 3:4). We cannot glorify God, especially while we are fallen under discipline, unless we discover our sins and confess them and perceive His wisdom in our discipline.

By those who are near and those who are far off he means Judah and Israel, for Israel was taken captive long ago and was scattered more than Judah. These were driven out of their lands because of treachery, so it was fitting for them not to lift up their faces, but in shame to confess to the Lord.
"O Lord, to us belongeth confusion of face, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against thee.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses, though we have rebelled against him" [8-9].

The prophet returns to complete his confession before God about himself and about the people with their leaders. Truly all deserved confusion of faces, especially the kings, the great men and the fathers. As it is said in Isaiah: "The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint. From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment" (Isa 1:6).
Neither have we obeyed the voice of the LORD our God, to walk in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law, even by departing, that they might not obey thy voice; therefore the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him" [10-11].
Israel committed two grave errors:

A. Disobedience to the law of God that was declared to them, and that was in their hands. There is nothing in it obscure or doubtful, for God declared His righteousness, His will and His commandments with all clarity through His laws. This makes the people deserve a double punishment.
B. They did not listen to the voice of the prophets who warned them [6].

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: Daniel did not try to justify the error of the people, but affirmed God's faithfulness in His promises and that He did not fall short toward His people. Once again he affirms that the transgression was collective. The curse was poured upon the people in all its classes like a flood that cannot be escaped. Here he uses the word "poured tittach", which is used of melting metals and pouring them over the bodies of criminals; such were the feelings of the captives concerning the bitterness of captivity and the deprivation of their land, their Temple and their freedom. And so their souls were bitter on account of God's disciplines of them. But God had warned them beforehand, stretching out His hands to them for long generations, indeed since the origin of this people in the days of Moses, their first leader. They are without excuse! The prophet also counted every sin, whatever its motive, as directed against God Himself [11].

St. Jerome comments on this phrase, saying: ["And Thou hast poured out upon us (the curse) drop by drop" (11 LXX), meaning: do not pour out upon us all Your wrath, for we cannot bear it, but pour out merely a drop of Your wrath, that we may return to You when we fall into Your net.]

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: "And he hath confirmed his words, which he spake against us, and against our judges that judged us, by bringing upon us a great evil: for under the whole heaven hath not been done as hath been done upon Jerusalem" [12].

It is as though the disciplines that befell the people are a confirmation of what He had foretold long ago by the tongue of the prophet Moses. He had warned beforehand not only the common people, but even those to whom He gave the right of judgment; for no one is above the divine law. No flesh may boast before God, and neither civil nor religious position exempts anyone from divine discipline. The leaders received authority from God, but within the limits of His law and His will. The authority granted by God does not cover their sins, nor does it protect them from discipline.
The period of captivity extended to seventy years, yet the people did not move to repentance, nor did they turn from their iniquities and accept the divine truth.

The Lord chose Jerusalem as a holy city for Himself, but when she sinned, disobeyed and persisted in not repenting, her discipline became great, such as had never been heard of before in all the world [12].

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: "As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil is come upon us: yet made we not our prayer before the LORD our God, that we might turn from our iniquities, and understand thy truth" [13].
The prophet Daniel confesses that the discipline of the Lord came upon them, and yet they did not benefit from this discipline, for the following reasons:

A. They did not make their prayer before the face of the Lord. Truly they practiced many prayers, whether those who remained in the cities of Israel and Judah or those who were taken captive; the priests, the leaders and the people practiced communal, individual and family prayers, but in the eyes of God these are not counted as supplication before the face of the Lord. They practiced outward formalities in hypocrisy, but their hearts did not rise toward heaven, nor did they enter into a living dialogue with God. Their prayers did not come from living faith, nor from a life of sincere repentance.
B. They did not turn from their iniquities, which deprived them of meeting with the Holy One and veiled their prayers from Him.

C. They did not understand God's truth, for they walked in worldly human wisdom and despised the divine wisdom. The scourges of discipline did not drive them to wisdom, but they remained in their folly. By saying: "that we might turn from our iniquities, and understand thy truth" [13], he links the holy life with the right faith or the divine truth; as he also links evil conduct with deviation from the truth. St. Jerome says: [Let the truth of God be counted equal to turning back from evil.]
The prophet links prayer or supplication before the face of the Lord with turning from iniquity together with the enjoyment of the divine wisdom springing from the divine truth.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: "Therefore hath the LORD watched upon the evil, and brought it upon us: for the LORD our God is righteous in all his works which he doeth: for we obeyed not his voice" [14].

"Watched" seked the Lord; this verb is used to mean wakefulness of mind and care for everything, and therefore it is used of the guards who watch night and day in vigilance to guard the cities. It is used here to declare that the calamities that occurred did not come by chance, but God, the Guardian of the soul and the One who cares for its salvation, permits in His wisdom that tribulation, or what we think to be evil, should come. He prolonged His longsuffering for long generations, and at the proper time He permitted the captivity for the edification of His people by discipline, even if it seemed harsh.

* Whenever we are rebuked for our sins, God watches over us and visits us with discipline. But when God leaves us alone and we suffer no discipline, we are unworthy of the Lord's rebuke, and for this reason it is said that He sleeps. We read well in the Psalms: "Then the Lord awaked as one out of sleep, and like a mighty man that shouteth by reason of wine" (Ps 78).

St. Jerome says that throughout the whole book Daniel affirmed the danger of believing that the tribulation that befalls us comes by accident as the result of random events. For there is no such thing as luck, but all things proceed through the hand of God, the Governor of all; otherwise we would have robbed God of His surpassing care for His creation, and wronged His power and His justice.

In the midst of our tribulation he wants to affirm that He is "the LORD our God", who cares for us, and it is fitting for us to hear His voice; that is, to understand His plan and listen to His teachings, not only through the commandments, but also through discipline and pain! He brings us into the school of discipline and reveals to us the philosophy of suffering!

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: "And now, O Lord our God, that hast brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and hast gotten thee renown, as at this day; we have sinned, we have done wickedly [15].

Since the prophet Daniel confessed his sins and the sins of his people, and confessed that they justly fell under discipline, he declares his trust in God the Savior of His people, for he carried the experience of salvation when He brought the people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand; now He is able to bring them out of Babylon, that His holy name may be glorified. The prophet Daniel believed that the God who worked in the past is still working now.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: "O Lord, according to all thy mercy, turn away thine anger and thy fury from thy city Jerusalem, thy holy mountain: because for our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and thy people are become a reproach to all that are about us" [16].
Though our sins are great and our evils many and we deserve death hundreds of times, yet Your mercies are also beyond number, and so we ask for "all" Your mercy.

As we enter boldly before the throne of Your mercy, turn away Your wrath from Your city in which we take pride, and from Your holy mountain which You chose that we might be sanctified in it, for upon it we offer to You the sacrifices acceptable before You.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: "Now therefore, O our God, hear the prayer of thy servant, and his supplications, and cause thy face to shine upon thy sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord's sake" [17].

It is as though he says to Him: Give us the proof of Your reconciliation with us by the shining of the light of Your face upon us, that we may be enlightened by You. He did not ask God to permit them to build the Temple that had been destroyed, but that He should shine with His light upon the Temple, for the house of the Lord is not built with stones, but by His dwelling in it and His pleasure in His people.

He closes the prayer with a request for God's swift intervention, not out of a sense of worthiness but for the sake of the grace of God. He did not ask God for mercy for his own sake, nor for the sake of Israel, but for the sake of God Himself, that His name may be glorified when the Gentiles see His wonders with them. Daniel found nothing to offer God to justify the enjoyment of His mercies, but he finds in the loving God the possibility of giving generously.
"All the mercy of God" [16]... for the mercies of God are great [18], and wide, and forgive all our sins and our disobedience.

· "For the sake of the city of God, the mountain of His holiness" [16], for it has become a reproach because of our sins, but it is the city of God and the mountain of His holiness. Here appear the feelings of the Apostle of severe deprivation and bitterness, because the city of God and the holy Temple occupy his heart, and he has been deprived of them.
· "For the Lord's sake" [17], that is, for the sake of God Himself.
· "For His name's sake", which is called upon the people and upon the city.

"O my God, incline thine ear, and hear; open thine eyes, and behold our desolations, and the city which is called by thy name: for we do not present our supplications before thee for our righteousnesses, but for thy great mercies.
O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do;

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: defer not, for thine own sake, O my God: for thy city and thy people are called by thy name" [18-19].

He does not ask God to listen to him and to look upon the desolation that has befallen the city, but asks that God incline His ear to him, and open His eyes to see. For when we sin we feel as though God ignores us completely, turns His ears away so as not to hear, and closes His eyes so as not to see. By saying this it is as though he says: "We want You, before You hear and see, to cling to us. We see You inclining Your ears like a father who bends down toward his child, and opening Your eyes with love, so that our souls find rest. We want You! Draw near to us, for we are in need of You." And St. Jerome says: [When He turns away His face we appear unworthy of the attention of His eyes or His ears.]

Throughout the period of captivity the people felt as though God had forsaken them, and no longer heard them, nor listened, nor worked on their behalf. Now Daniel asks in the name of the people that He forgive without delay, for they ask to enjoy His goodness and His mercies.

entries.section: D. The sense of sharing his people's sins:

paragraphs.text: Thus Daniel offered God reasons to have mercy on His people, imitating Moses who used to intercede for the people. Daniel did not justify himself, but felt responsible as a member of this community, and that he has a positive role to which he is committed. Truly the Scripture does not mention any personal sins that Daniel committed, but this does not prevent him from repenting together with the people collectively, for he says: "confessing my sin and the sin of my people" [20].
Because the prophet Daniel was a man of prayer, he enjoyed the following blessings:
A. The appearance of the Son of Man to him more than once (Dan 7:13; 8:15; 10:5-9). Thus Daniel enjoyed Him who is the desire of the nations.

B. Daniel's being alone in seeing surpassing heavenly visions, for he says: "And I Daniel alone saw the vision: for the men that were with me saw not the vision; but a great quaking fell upon them, so that they fled to hide themselves. Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision" (Dan 10:7-8).

C. He enjoyed the company of the archangel Gabriel, whom the Son of Man asked to interpret the visions to him and make him understand the mysteries of His first and last coming and His work of salvation (Dan 8:16; 9:21; 11:1), and who also used to strengthen him (Dan 10:19).
D. He was called the man greatly beloved of God (Dan 9:23; 10:19). The literal meaning is "the man whom God desires and delights in".

20 And whiles I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before the LORD my God for the holy mountain of my God; 21 Yea, whiles I was speaking in prayer, even the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation. 22 And he informed me, and talked with me, and said, "O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding. 23 At the beginning of thy supplications the commandment came forth, and I am come to shew thee; for thou art greatly beloved: therefore understand the matter, and consider the vision.
"And whiles I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before the LORD my God for the holy mountain of my God" [20].

St. Augustine often quoted this verse in his discourse against the followers of Pelagius and Coelestius, who relied on human work and ignored divine grace and the asking for divine mercies. St. Augustine always affirmed that there is not one righteous man in the world who does not need the mercies of God. If Daniel, of whom the Holy Bible mentions no sin that he committed, and to whom Ezekiel bore witness as one of three persons in the world of renown, "Job, Noah and Daniel" (Ezek 14:14), threw himself into the flock of sinners, asking in humility and contrition for the forgiveness of his sins, what then shall be our state?! The Lord Christ required all His disciples to ask every day for the forgiveness of sins more than once in the Lord's Prayer, so whoever thinks that he is righteous and has no need of forgiveness separates himself from the school of the Lord Christ.

St. Jerome says: [As we have already pointed out before, Daniel did not think only of the sins of the people but also of his own sins, as being one of the people, or he did this by way of humility, for even if he had not committed personal sins, his aim was to obtain pardon by his humility.]
"Yea, whiles I was speaking in prayer, even the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening oblation.
And he informed me, and talked with me, and said,
O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding.
At the beginning of thy supplications the commandment came forth, and I am come to shew thee; for thou art greatly beloved:
therefore understand the matter, and consider the vision [21-23].

The prophet Daniel reveals the surpassing love of God, who listens to his prayer, accepts his confession of his sins and the sins of his people, and hearkens to his supplication for the holy mountain of the Lord, that is, for the city of Jerusalem, the Temple and all the divine holy things.
God delights in the humble believers who confess their weaknesses, and who in burning zeal do not ask for themselves, but for others, as for the divine holy things.

First: The prophet Daniel says: "whiles I was speaking" [21]. Daniel did not pray with his heart only, but also with his tongue; he offers prayer with his spirit as with his body; he shares with his whole being in expressing what is in his depths. And the answer to his question came to him while he was praying.

Second: The prophet Daniel had not yet finished his prayer, for he says: "whiles I was speaking in prayer" [21]; God answered his prayer before he finished it. And the wonder is that the archangel Gabriel says to him: "At the beginning of thy supplications the commandment came forth" [23], that is, at the start of the prayer, because God answered Daniel's heart before he expressed what was in it with his lips.

Third: God sent to him an archangel flying swiftly! A wonderful divine concern. Here for the first time we hear of the wings of angels or that they are flying beings. He appeared to him in the form of a man, therefore he said "the man Gabriel". By this God affirms His esteem for man and His pride in him, making His angels not only appear to serve man, but also bear his form, so that a meeting between them may be possible. St. Jerome says: [It is said that he "flew" because he appeared in the likeness of a man.]

Fourth: The archangel appeared to Daniel and touched him "about the time of the evening oblation", that is, at the third hour after noon. Daniel had been a captive for nearly seventy years and had not seen the evening sacrifice that the priests used to offer in the Temple of the Lord. But the long years did not draw his heart away from the sacrifice, and did not deprive him of enjoying the blessing of the house of the Lord whose stones had been thrown down! In the midst of the palace in Babylon his heart went forth with every morning and evening to share in spirit in the worship that had ceased in Jerusalem. Thus a man is joined with all the people in worship, even if he is shut away in a cell, and he shares in the surpassing worship of the heavenly Church wherever he may be.

St. Jerome says: [It is said: "about the time of the evening oblation" to show that the prayer of the prophet extended from the time of the morning sacrifice until the evening, and therefore God directed His mercy to him.]

The appearance of the archangel and his touch "at the time of the evening oblation" carries a symbolic meaning: that evening had come, and the fullness of time had arrived in which the seventy years of captivity do not end, but the time of sin ends with the coming of the Liberator and Savior, who touches us by His divine Incarnation and leads us into the new heavenly knowledge.

Fifth: The archangel Gabriel revealed to Daniel his standing with God, for he says: "for thou art greatly beloved" [23], and in the literal meaning of the Hebrew word "the man whom God desires", that is, the object of God's delight. God, who loves all mankind, takes the greatest pleasure in those who enjoy a deep fellowship with Him, and He delights to reveal to them His divine mysteries.

Sixth: He gave him a divine commandment, indeed a divine gift, which is the gift of understanding: "therefore understand the matter, and consider the vision" [23]. Daniel had studied the prophecies of Jeremiah and understood the date of the return from captivity, but he needed a greater understanding, in which his heart is drawn from the return to Canaan to the return to heaven itself through the work of the Messiah.

entries.section: 4. The vision of the seventy weeks:

paragraphs.text: 24 Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy. 25 Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks: the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times. 26 And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself: and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined. 27 And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate."

This vision has a special importance for the Jews as for the Christians, and both parties agree that the day here refers to a year, and the week to seven years. As it is said in the book of Leviticus: "And thou shalt number seven sabbaths of years unto thee, seven times seven years..." (Lev 25:8).

As for the aim of this vision, St. Jerome says that the teaching of the Jews before his time differs from the teaching of his contemporaries. The earlier ones in humility acknowledged that this passage cannot be understood except by the coming of the Messiah. But it is noticeable that most of the rabbis see in this vision that the divine punishment falls upon the Jews even after their return from captivity. In their opinion the seventy weeks begin with the destruction of the former Temple and end with the destruction of the second Temple in the days of Titus. As for the Christian Church, despite the differing opinions of the commentators and theologians, all agree that the center of the whole vision is the person of the Lord Christ, as we shall see in our explanation of the texts of the vision.

entries.section: First: the purpose of the vision:

paragraphs.text: "Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy" [24].

This period (seventy weeks) was determined for the achievement of a special purpose with six results, three of them negative and the other three positive, and all of these were actually fulfilled by the coming of the Lord Christ:

A. To finish the transgression, that is, to remove it from before the eyes of God, by the preaching of the Gospel of salvation and the enjoyment of the gift of the Holy Spirit which God gave to His Church by the merits of the precious Blood, so that our transgression has become as though it does not exist before God. The captivity was a discipline for the transgressions of Israel and Judah, but it was not a just punishment for them, and the captivity has no power to blot out sin and remove it, therefore there was need of the sacrifice of the Cross, where the Lord Christ offers Himself as an atonement for the sins of the whole world (1 Jn 2:1).

B. To make an end of sins, and it is translated "ending". For the Lord Christ offered Himself as a sin offering once for the whole world, He in whom there is no blemish in soul or in body, and put an end to sin.
C. To make reconciliation for iniquity, and this implies that necessity required the offering of a sacrifice of reconciliation or atonement.

These are the negative results, in which the curse of transgression, sins and iniquity is removed, which veiled us from God and brought us into enmity so that we needed reconciliation. Now he tells us of the three positive results.

D. To bring in everlasting righteousness, which brings lasting peace, for the Messiah brings it and offers it as a divine gift; He offers Himself as righteousness so that we are justified by Him. Righteousness is brought to us from outside our nature, for it is the work of God in us through the righteous Messiah.

And St. Athanasius the Apostolic, commenting on the prophecy of the prophet Daniel in this chapter, says: [This is the reason for all their prophecies, I mean until the true Righteous One should come, He who became a ransom for the sins of all.] As St. Paul the Apostle says: "Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification" (1 Cor 1:30). Montgomery, who adopted the views of the modern critics, when he cited some of the opinions of Jewish scholars in the interpretation of this prophecy, mentioned that Rabbi Moses Haddershan says: "Everlasting righteousness is the King Messiah".

E. To seal up the vision and prophecy, for the prophecies of the Old Testament and the visions contained in it are fulfilled by the coming of the Messiah, and the declaration of His person, His redemptive work and His eternal glory. Daniel and other prophets enjoyed visions and prophecies on behalf of the people of God, but a time comes when there is no need of this, when the Word of God Himself dwells in our midst and speaks with us mouth to mouth.
And as Pope Athanasius says, when the Lord Christ came there was no longer any need of prophecies and visions among the Jews.
[For when did prophecy and vision cease from Israel, except when Christ came, the Most Holy?

For this is a sign and a strong proof of the coming of the Word of God, that Jerusalem no longer stands, no prophet arises any more, and no vision is declared to them; this is very natural. For what was meant has come, so what need is there any longer for any indication of Him? When the truth has come, what need is there any longer for the shadow...?
Thus, when the Most Holy by nature came, the vision and prophecy were sealed up and the kingdom of Jerusalem ended.

The kings were anointed from among them only until the Most Holy came, who was anointed. Jacob prophesies concerning the kingdom of the Jews that it is established until His coming, for it was said: "A ruler (sceptre) shall not depart from Judah, nor a prince (lawgiver) from between his feet, until he come (Shiloh), and he whom the nations expect" (see Gen 49:10). And the Savior Himself cried out, saying: "For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John" (Mt 11:13; Lk 16:16). If there were now among the Jews a king or a prophet or a vision, they would be right to deny that Christ has come.]

F. To anoint the Most Holy, for He sanctified Himself for us, offering Himself as High Priest and a unique sacrifice and an intercessor for us. As the Lord Christ says in His farewell prayer: "And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth" (Jn 17:19). It is as though He has no aim except to bring every soul into the eternal glories and the enjoyment of the heavenly inheritance. In another translation, "to anoint the Holy of Holies", that is, to anoint the place of utmost holiness, the most holy place in the Temple.

St. Jerome observed that God says to the prophet Daniel: "thy people, thy holy city" and did not say: "my people, my holy city", because God had divorced His people and rejected His city because of their transgressions. So God spoke with the prophet Moses when the people were persisting in sin. And perhaps here God declares to Daniel, who loves his Jewish people and the city of Jerusalem, that when the Lord Christ comes and accomplishes salvation, His own will not receive Him, and will not believe in Him, so they become a rejected people and a city under discipline!

entries.section: Second: the three stages of the seventy weeks:

paragraphs.text: "Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks: the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times.
And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself: and the people
of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined.

And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate" [24-27].

God determined a definite time for the coming of the incarnate Word of God into the world, and with surpassing wisdom determined the hour in which the Messiah would be born, and the moment in which He would offer His life as an atonement for the sins of the world, for the coming of the Lord and His saving work are in the eyes of God the center of history, the nerve of divine providence, and the crown of grace. Nothing happens by chance, but everything is accomplished with wonderful precision. The Holy Bible has affirmed the coming of the Savior in the fullness of time at the end of the ages.

This prophecy came like a shining star in the midst of the sorrows of the captives who suffered the darkness of deadly grief. Many understood the prophecy, so that when He came there was a general expectation among the Jews of the coming of the Messiah. Holy men and women studied the prophecies diligently, and awaited the coming of the Savior. Simeon the elder was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and Anna was looking for salvation in Jerusalem with others who held the same thought. Not only the Jews, but the Samaritans also expected His coming soon, as appears from the words of the Samaritan woman: "I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ" (Jn 4:25). Even among the Gentiles some awaited His coming, as happened with the Magi who saw His star.

The scholar Tertullian, in his treatise "An Answer to the Jews", chapter 8, gave a detailed presentation of how this prophecy was fulfilled exactly in the birth of the Lord Christ, His sufferings and the destruction of Jerusalem.

* Concerning this point (the coming of the Lord Christ), their opinions are refuted, rather, not by our hands, but by those of the very wise Daniel, who determined both the actual date of the coming of the Savior and His divine dwelling among us, saying: "Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people..." Perhaps with regard to the other prophecies they can find excuses and postpone what is written to the future. But what can they say about this (prophecy), or how can they confront it completely? For it not only points to Christ, but declares that He who is anointed is not a mere man but the Most Holy, and that Jerusalem stands until His coming, and then prophecy and vision cease in Israel.

St. Athanasius the Apostolic. His Grace Anba Dioscorus comments on this chapter, saying that, because of the precision and clarity of this chapter in determining the time of the crucifixion of the Lord Christ after His Incarnation, the Jews changed the expression "to anoint the Most Holy" to "the dedication of the Holy of Holies" in the copy in circulation among them under the name of the Masoretic, whose date they trace to the eleventh century AD, so that the prophecy might appear to concern a place and not a person; indeed they placed the book of Daniel in the section of the Ketubim, which contains the historical books, the Psalms and the heavenly books of wisdom, so that it should not be counted among the prophetic books. This was proclaimed by some scholars.

And Fr. Bishoy Kamel comments on this prophecy, saying: [In truth these calculations gave the Jews the opportunity to know the time of the coming of the Messiah approximately. Therefore our teacher Luke the Evangelist says: "... waiting for the consolation of Israel,... redemption in Jerusalem" (Lk 2:25, 38). Indeed some thought "that the kingdom of God should immediately appear" (Lk 19:11). Therefore the Jews became without excuse in determining the time of the coming of the Lord Christ.]

entries.section: Third: what is the meaning of the week?

paragraphs.text: The word "week" here came in Hebrew "shabua Shabua", derived from "seba", not in the sense of seven days, but a unit of seven. The plural of the word came "shabu'im Shabu'im", which is not the usual feminine plural of the word for week, and therefore it means sevens or periods of seven. The scholars and commentators of the Jews and Christians have agreed in their interpretation of this prophecy, despite the difference of their approaches, that the phrase "seventy weeks" means seventy units of sevens, and thus it means seventy weeks of years. The majority of commentators held that this period begins somewhere between (457 and 445 BC) and ends somewhere between (26 and 70 AD).

entries.section: Fourth: the decrees concerning the return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple and Jerusalem:

paragraphs.text: Three decrees or royal commands were issued concerning the return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple and Jerusalem:

The first decree: issued by Cyrus in 538 BC or 537 BC, after his taking of Babylon (Isa 44:8; 45:1; Ezra 1:1-2; 2 Chr 36:22-23). The first return began under the leadership of Zerubbabel, and the restoration of the altar and the reorganization of worship began, but the enemies opposed them. In the reign of Darius I the decree of Cyrus was searched for, and the king commanded that the work continue (from 520 to 515 BC). It is fitting for us to notice that Cyrus issued a command to build the Temple only, but did not issue a command to restore the city of Jerusalem and build it. The prophet Daniel says that it is from the issuing of the command to restore Jerusalem and build it, which is different from the issuing of the command to build the Temple.
