There is a great difference between the two commands, for Cyrus saw no objection to helping the Jews build the Temple, as a matter of policy on his part, but he saw that helping them build the city and restore its fortifications was a danger to him. The building of the Temple is considered the end of the period of captivity, which is 70 years. The command of the king was recorded in the book of (Ezra 1:2-3): "Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD God of Israel, (he is the God,) which is in Jerusalem." There is not a word in this command about restoring the city and building it.

The second decree: issued by King Artaxerxes I (464-424 BC) in 457 BC and carried by Ezra the priest and scribe (Ezra 8) about 80 years after the first return. The decree permitted those of the Jews who wished to return to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:13); the organization of the judiciary and the application of the law of Moses (Ezra 7:7); and the arrangement of the financial matters of the Temple (Ezra 7:15, 20). Ezra's concern was the rebuilding of the people themselves morally and spiritually (Dan 7:9). He was given the right to restore the building of the Temple and to set up the walls, for he said: "For we were bondmen; yet our God hath not forsaken us in our bondage, but hath extended mercy unto us in the sight of the kings of Persia, to give us a reviving, to set up the house of our God, and to repair the desolations thereof, and to give us a wall in Judah and in Jerusalem" (Ezra 9:9). Unfortunately history has not given us anything about the reforms that took place concerning the building, but it is clear that Ezra carried out the moral and spiritual reform and was not able to build the walls or restore the city. This appears from what Hanani said later to Nehemiah: "The remnant that are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire" (Neh 1:3). It is clear from Nehemiah's behavior in the same chapter that he did not expect the condition of Jerusalem to be so, perhaps because he expected that Ezra and those with him had carried out restorations in the city and built the walls.

The third decree: issued by Artaxerxes I in Nisan of the twentieth year of his reign (March/April 445 BC), carried by Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer (Neh 1:11), and Nehemiah built the wall of Jerusalem and built the city, for he says to the king: "If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers' sepulchres, that I may build it" (Neh 2:5).

entries.section: Fifth: the calculations of the three stages:

paragraphs.text: The prophet Daniel asked - in faith - that God fulfill His promises, which were the return of the people after seventy years of captivity; and behold, God offered him what is greater, to be accomplished not after 70 years but after its sabbaths (70 × 7 = 490 years), so that he and all mankind might enjoy a new Sabbath, and surpassing rest and the righteousness of God, which He prepared for them through the generations, and which the fathers and prophets longed for, namely the return of mankind to God through the saving work of God. This is by the Incarnation of the Word and the offering of Himself as an atonement for the sins of the world. He determined the time of the coming of this Savior and His crucifixion, as He also revealed the events of His last coming.
* This phrase stands thus, for it touches many wonders...

It is clear that the phrase speaks of the coming of Christ, who had to declare Himself after seventy weeks. For in the time of the Savior transgressions were removed and sins came to an end, and iniquities were blotted out through forgiveness, together with transgressions, by the atonement, and the everlasting righteousness, which differs from the righteousness of the Law, was preached, and the visions and prophecies (ceased) until John, and the Most Holy was anointed. For these things were not accomplished before the coming of the Savior, but they were hoping for them.

The angel teaches us that the beginning of the numbers, that is, the seventy weeks which are 490 years, begins with the command issued to begin the building of Jerusalem (in response to the request of the captives). This happened in the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia. For Nehemiah asked him and received the answer that Jerusalem must be built... That was in the year 115 of the Persian Empire and the fourth year of the 83rd Olympiad, and the twentieth year of Artaxerxes himself.

To this date, which is the second year of the 202nd Olympiad and the 16th year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar (in which the Lord Christ was crucified), the sum is 475 years, which corresponds to 490 years by the Jewish reckoning, since they reckon the year according to the cycle of the moon. This is easy to show, for their year consists of 354 days while the solar year consists of 365 and a quarter days, so that the last year exceeds, in the 12 months according to the cycle of the moon, by 11 and a quarter days...

Fr. Julius Africanus: [Between the fourth year of the 83rd Olympiad and the second year of the 202nd Olympiad, where the Olympiad is held every 4 years, the sum is 475 solar years, which is equivalent to 490 lunar years.]
St. Jerome cited the opinion of Fr. Julius Africanus Julius Africanus in his interpretation of this vision.

First: 7 weeks, that is, 7×7=49 years, the period between the issuing of the command to repair the Temple and build the wall by the edict of Artaxerxes I on 14 Nisan (March - April) in the year 445 BC, and the appointment of Nehemiah as governor over Jerusalem, and the period ended in the year 397 or 396 BC, when Nehemiah died in the days of the prophet Malachi. The seven weeks [that is, 49 years] are the period of the restoration of Jerusalem and its building, because it was worn-out ruins. There is no doubt that Nehemiah spent this period in building Jerusalem, and the last of his work in his governorship over Jerusalem was the organization of the affairs of the Israelite nation and the reform of its affairs. Nehemiah was appointed governor over Judea and did not complete the restoration of Jerusalem except during the period of his second governorship. For the first time he continued 12 years as governor over Judea, because Artaxerxes issued to him a command to build Jerusalem and appointed him governor over it. And in the thirty-second year Nehemiah returned to him, then asked the king's permission to return to Jerusalem (Neh 13:6-7), and he permitted him. It is no secret that Nehemiah lived long; if his age when he began the restoration of Jerusalem was 30 years, and he spent 49 years in building it, his age was 79 years, and the historian Josephus said that he was aged.

Some give a calculation for the building of the Temple during 49 years as follows: Cyrus permitted the people to build the Temple, and they laid the foundations in three years when Cyrus went to war in Scythia Scythis, but the Jews were forced to stop building in the days of his successor Cambyses Cambyses, who was hostile to them. And when they were permitted to build, they completed it in 46 years; in this period (3 + 46 = 49 years) Jerusalem was restored, and likewise the state of the Jewish people, religiously and civilly, by Ezra and Nehemiah.

Second: 62 weeks (62 × 7 = 434 years). This period, which amounts to four centuries, represents the darkest periods of the people spiritually, for there were no prophets in it until the appearance of St. John the Baptist. They were rightly counted as sitting in darkness until the Sun of Righteousness should rise upon them by His Cross.

* After the return of the people from Babylon under the leadership of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, Ezra the scribe and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel of the tribe of David (and the restoration of Jerusalem and its building) there are 434 years until the coming of the Lord Christ, when the High Priest of priests appears to the world, and there rises clearly the One who takes away sin from the world, as John says of Him: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." But who is this who blots out our transgressions? Paul the Apostle teaches us, saying: "For he is our peace, who hath made both one" (Eph 2:14); and then "Blotting out the handwriting of our sins that was against us" (Col 2:14).
There are 434 years between the return of the people from Babylon (and the restoration of Jerusalem and its building) and the time of the birth of the Lord Christ. This can easily be perceived.
St. Hippolytus of Rome: In this period two important events took place:

The first event is the appearance of Antiochus Epiphanes (167-164 BC), who is considered the "antichrist" in the Old Testament, he who stopped the offering of the daily burnt sacrifice for three and a half years, and appointed Greek priests who introduced the worship of the Greek gods, and defiled the Temple with the blood of a swine and killed thousands of the Jews, but the Maccabees withstood him until the Temple was freed and the burnt offering returned.

The second event is in the days of the Roman Empire, when Herod the Great reigned, who wished to win the favor of the Jews, and began the building of the new Temple about the year 20 BC. Its building took 46 years; and he had enlarged the Temple area to nearly double the space.

Since it is stated in [27] that the abolition of the animal sacrifice is in the midst of the week, that is, in the midst of the last week of the 69 weeks, this means that the crucifixion takes place in week 68.5, that is, after (68.5 × 7) 479.5 years from the issuing of the edict for the work of restoring the Temple by Nehemiah (in 445 BC), so that the crucifixion is 33 and a half years after the birth, and this was fulfilled, for the Lord Christ was crucified at this age. As for the end of the last week, it is about 35 years after the crucifixion (3.5 days), that is, about the year 70 AD, when the Temple was completely demolished at the hands of Titus the Roman.

Some scholars hold that the crucifixion of the Lord Christ came 483 years (7 + 62 = 69 × 7 = 483) after the issuing of the edict of Artaxerxes mentioned above. Because the crucifixion took place in April of the year 30 AD, if the edict was issued in 445 BC, the difference is 445 BC + 30 = 475 years and not 483, so there is a difference of 8 years. The reason for these eight years is that the year in the Holy Bible is reckoned as 360 days and not like the astronomical or Julian year of 365 and a quarter days. The five and a quarter days in the year cause a difference of 8 years. Thus the coming of the Messiah the Prince was fulfilled exactly after 69 weeks (69 × 7 = 483 years), reckoning the year as it is in the Holy Bible.

Gleason L. Archer holds that the 69 symbolic years (483 years) are reckoned from the second decree, or the first decree with respect to King Artaxerxes I in 457 BC, which was carried by Ezra the scribe for the building, even though the building was accomplished only by Nehemiah. If we subtract 483 from 457 BC, 26 remains, and since there is no year equal to zero, the number 1 is added to 26, so that the date is 27 AD. And since it is known that the Lord Christ was crucified in 30 AD, He would have begun His ministry and His baptism in 27 AD. Thus the prophecy was fulfilled exactly.

Others hold that the twentieth year of Artaxerxes is the year 454 BC, according to the investigations of the scholars Hengstenberg and Ussher. If we subtract this period from the product of 69 weeks multiplied by 7 (483 years), which is the period the prophet Daniel spoke of in verse 25, the remainder is about 29 AD, which is the beginning of the ministry of the Lord Christ, or His call to the way of salvation, for it is the very goal intended, because the important point in the dates of kings and sultans is the beginning of their reign and work, and not their birth; therefore the prophet Daniel observed this very point that was intended.

Thus many hold that this second period ends with the baptism of the Lord Christ and the beginning of His preaching of His Gospel, so that the third period comes, in which the Lord Christ offers His sacrifice in the midst of the week, that is, after three and a half years of His ministry, and the animal sacrifices are abolished.

entries.section: Third: the seventieth week, or the last week.

paragraphs.text: "And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease..." [27].

There is an opinion or meditation in the interpretation of this verse that this week refers to the week of the Passion with its seven days, when the Lord Christ entered the Temple on Sunday (the tenth of Nisan) as a lamb and drove out the sheep that symbolized Him, and continued to stay overnight in Bethany as though under guard until the fourteenth day (Thursday), when He kept the last Passover with His disciples and abolished it, and it was the supper at which He offered to His disciples the sacrifice of the New Covenant, with His Body and Blood changed from the bread and wine, as a rite after the order of Melchizedek according to the prophecy of the prophet David in the Psalm. The first five days refer to the five thousand years (approximately) in which the bloody sacrifices that symbolized Him were offered, then the remaining two days of the week to the two thousand years, and thus the saying of Peter the Apostle is fulfilled when he speaks of the second coming of the Lord Christ for judgment, saying: "But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.. etc." (2 Pet 3:8-10).

Some hold that the 69 weeks ended with the Lord Christ's offering of Himself as a unique sacrifice of love, and now the vision of Daniel carries us to the end of the world, which is the period of the last seven years in which the Antichrist comes to reign for three and a half years, when there is the great tribulation of which the Lord Christ spoke: "When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:) Then let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains: Let him which is on the housetop not come down to take any thing out of his house... For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened (Mt 24:15-21). And He spoke after that of His last coming.

Daniel also spoke of it in another place: "and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time" (Dan 12:1). And in Jeremiah: "Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob's trouble; but he shall be saved out of it" (Jer 30:7); and it is stated in Zephaniah: "Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of the LORD's wrath; but the whole land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy" (Zeph 1:18).

And it is stated in the book of Revelation: "These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (Rev 7:14). The description of this period of tribulation is given in (Rev 6:15; 11:1-14; 12:6-17).

* By the stretching out of His hands he means His sufferings, and by the reference to a time, times and half a time he indicates the three and a half years of the Antichrist... which are the 1290 days that Daniel prophesied for the ending of the suffering and the accomplishment of the scattering when the Antichrist comes.
St. Hippolytus of Rome
You grant me more than I ask,
In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a thing was revealed unto Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar;
and the thing was true, but the time appointed was long: and he understood the thing, and had understanding of the vision [1].

In the third year of the reign of Cyrus king of Persia. Comparing this with what is stated in (Dan 1:21), "And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus", we understand that Daniel was retired and left the service at the age of eighty, one year after Cyrus took the kingdom.

As for the reason why he did not return to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel but remained in Babylon, the Scripture does not tell us; perhaps it was by a divine command, that he might fulfil a special mission of serving his people, which he carried out while in the land of captivity.

This vision was granted to him two years after he left his work, shortly before his repose. It was confirmed that God would surely fulfil what he saw (Rev 22:6), for he says, "the thing was true"; there is no room for doubt, even though the events were unexpected. In any case, Daniel determined that the appointed time was long. Some see that the time is long because the fourth vision (ch. 10-12) extends to the resurrection of the dead and the end of the age.
Concerning the previous vision Daniel was perplexed and unable to understand it, but of this prophecy he affirms that he understood it fully.
Why does he mention here his name that was given to him in Babylon, "Belteshazzar"?

a. To affirm that although he had been retired and was no longer present in the palace, no one knew him by his original name; rather, the name that had been imposed upon him clung to him, and although he did not love the name, he left it, hoping to find through it an opportunity to serve his people.
b. Although he still bore this Chaldean name all this time, his heart still clung to his God, who revealed His secrets to him and granted him understanding and wisdom.

entries.section: a. A period of fasting and mourning:

paragraphs.text: "In those days I Daniel was mourning three full weeks. I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, till three whole weeks were fulfilled" [2].

Daniel fasted three full weeks, eating no pleasant food and not anointing himself with oil, because Cyrus was occupied with the war against the Scythians, and so he left the region of Asia Minor, and his son Cambyses (Campyses) opposed the rebuilding of the Temple and of the holy city Jerusalem. Indeed, some had returned to the Promised Land, but they were in disgrace and shame, unable to restore the spiritual life in their country. Perhaps he also heard of the indifference of those who returned to Jerusalem concerning the building of the Temple, the house of the Lord.
He distinguishes between the week in the previous vision, as a symbol of seven years, and the week here, for he calls it "a week of days", that is, in its literal sense and not its symbolic one.

In the first chapter of the book we saw him abstaining from the king's delicacies, content with eating pulse. Did he go back to eating meat and drinking wine? The text does not mean this; rather, in addition to his earlier abstaining from the king's delicacies, he now refuses all pleasant food even in his own house, to offer a strict fast on behalf of his people.

Some attack the fasting of the Church as though it had no purpose, and say that there is no need for it except in necessity, as happened here with Daniel the prophet. The answer to this is that Daniel was a man of prayer together with fasting from the time the first chapter presented his life to us. Indeed his fasting had its purpose, and so did his prayer, but we never heard that he ceased praying until, when affliction came, he prayed. He presented to us his prayer and confession in a time of distress, and this did not keep him from praying three times a day. So it is with the fasting of the Church: we need it alongside the special fasts when certain afflictions come. What must be stressed, however, is the existence of a clear spiritual purpose, not for the Church's fasts only, but for all our worship.

Along with abstaining from meat and wine, Daniel the prophet also abstained from all pleasant food. So it is fitting for us in our fasts, along with abstaining from animal products, to abstain from all pleasant food, even if it is vegetarian, so that we do not eat with desire, even if it is dry bread.

Daniel's fasting was joined to prayer and confession of his sins, because fasting is a preparation of the soul for speaking with its God, and is not a goal in itself. The Lord linked the two when He said, "Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting" (Mt 17:21).

* In any case, since Daniel, the man of desires, exercised control over his passions, he gained control over the kingdom of the Chaldeans: he cast down their idols, destroyed the dragon, tamed the lions, preached the Incarnation, and interpreted the hidden mysteries (Dan 5:9, 14).
St. Basil the Great * And what of Daniel? How did he receive the contemplation of wonders? Was it not after a fast of twenty days?!

entries.section: a. A period of fasting and mourning:

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great "And in the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel" [4].

Some see that he saw himself in the vision on the bank of the river Tigris, though he was not actually there, nor dwelling in that region; while others see that after three weeks of fasting Daniel was beside the great river (the Tigris), walking on the bank of the river, contemplating God and His dealings, as Isaac used to walk in the field.

At the river Chebar the prophet Ezekiel saw his great vision (Ezek 1), and at the streams of the Jordan the heavens were opened to see our Lord and Savior being baptized... So when we sit beside the waters of Baptism, and receive the work of God's Spirit in us, and realize our sonship to God, we receive a new vision in our depths, and discover the transfiguration of the only-begotten Son of God in our depths. We see Him as one upon His throne, granting us the pledge of His heavenly glory until we meet Him face to face and enjoy fellowship in His glories and His eternal inheritance.

Instead of the feast Daniel was sad and fasting, eating no meat and drinking no wine, and not anointing himself with oil as the Persians were accustomed to do. The vision appeared to him while he was in mourning, weeping over the sins of his people.

Two years earlier Cyrus had permitted those of the Jews who wished to return to Jerusalem, but few accepted this. For many preferred to remain in Babylon carrying on their trade and attending to material gain, rather than spending what they had on returning with their families to begin new projects in the Promised Land. This is what grieved Daniel the prophet, who remained in captivity, not out of greed for position or gain, but to serve those who had not yet returned. Perhaps what also grieved him was that he heard of the slackness of those who had returned to Jerusalem in building the house of the Lord, being concerned with building their own houses, reckoning that the time had not yet come to build. This also grieved the heart of the prophet Haggai, when the word of the Lord came to him: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" (Hag 1:4).
This vision came on the four and twentieth day of the first month, that is, during the feast of unleavened bread (Ex 12:18), which comes directly after the Passover and lasts for a week.
"Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz:

entries.section: a. A period of fasting and mourning:

paragraphs.text: His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude" [5-6].

Some see that the word Uphaz is an adjective meaning "pure", while others see that it refers to a certain region, as it is written in Jeremiah, "gold from Uphaz" (Jer 10:9), and some translate it "Ophir".

Some see that the linen garment here signifies the priesthood of the Lord Christ, and the golden girdle the pastoral work of the Lord Christ. For it was the custom in the East to wear girdles about the loins, because their garments were long, reaching to the feet, and hindered their movement. So the girdle lifts up the garment and helps a person to serve and to move quickly.

His body was like the beryl, and as St. Jerome says: [It is one of the twelve precious stones set on the breastplate of the high priest. If the precious stones signify the twelve tribes, the high priest stands before God interceding for them, and carries them in love upon his breast that they may enjoy the divine presence. But we, having become one tribe, belong to the tribe of Judah (spiritually), and have become members in the body of the Lord Christ. So we do not find ourselves upon the breastplate of the Savior, but rather members of His body, having the right to enter the heavenly sanctuaries with the heavenly Head.

His voice was like the voice of a great multitude; Daniel the prophet heard it and understood it, while those who were with him fled and understood nothing of the voice. This is what happened with Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus, where he saw and heard, and spoke with Jesus Christ, who appeared to him from heaven, while those around him saw as though they had not seen, and heard a voice and understood nothing; therefore they were counted as though they had not seen and had not heard (Acts 9:7; 22:9).

Daniel the prophet beheld a person whose description matches what is said of the Lord Christ in the Revelation of St. John the Theologian (Rev 1:13-15). Some see that he beheld a mighty angel, while others see that it was the Word of God before the Incarnation. For while he was mourning over the sins of his people, there appeared to him the One who bears the sins of the whole world.

* He says: "Then I lifted up (my eyes), and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen" [5]. In the first vision he says, "Behold, the angel Gabriel has been sent"; but here the matter is different, for he sees the Lord, not as a perfect man but in the form of a man...

His wearing a garment of various colors signifies symbolically the diversity of the graces of our calling. The priestly garment was made of different colors, because various nations were awaiting the coming of Christ, that we might become (one body) of contrasting colors.

He says, "and his loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz" [5]. The word "Uphaz" passed from Hebrew into Greek to mean pure gold. He girded his loins with a pure girdle. The "Word" had to carry us and bind us to Himself like a girdle around His body, by His own love, the perfect Body, while we are members of His body joined together, and we stand by the Word Himself.

"His body also was like Tharses (the beryl)". The word Tharses is interpreted "Ethiopians", or "hard to recognize". So the prophet proclaimed beforehand, affirming that the body would be revealed in the world, but that many would find it difficult to recognize it.

"And his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire". For it is fitting for the fiery power of the Word and for judgment that He should announce beforehand His exercise of fire (His judgment), shining with justice upon the wicked and destroying them.

He adds also these words: "and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass" to show the first and second calling of men, that is, of the Gentiles. "For the others shall be as the former"; for your rulers are set up as at the beginning. "And the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude" (Isa 1:26; Rev 19:6). For we all utter things that were prophesied; we speak by His mouth of the things that He Himself appointed.
St. Hippolytus of Rome "And I Daniel alone saw the vision: for the men that were with me saw not the vision; but a great quaking fell upon them, so that they fled to hide themselves.
Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength.

entries.section: a. A period of fasting and mourning:

paragraphs.text: Yet heard I the voice of his words: and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I in a deep sleep on my face, and my face toward the ground" [7-9].

Daniel, the best man of his time, realized that his perfection had turned, as it were, into corruption, and so he did not boast of self-righteousness, which is counted as filthy rags (Isa 64:6). Since the glory of the Lord overcame him, the prophet fell to the ground like one who had lost consciousness and whose strength had utterly failed, yet he perceived the voice of the Lord.

Fear fell on those who were with Daniel the prophet and they fled to hide themselves; perhaps they saw something strange, but they did not discern the vision, so they were terrified. God allowed them this lest anyone think that what Daniel declared was an illusion or imagination. He was chosen above others to become a teacher who reveals the secrets of God and receives divine knowledge on behalf of the whole congregation, but he needed someone to bear witness to him that he was called to a sublime divine work.
He repeated more than once that he saw, to affirm that what he utters is a reality he truly beheld, and he calls the vision great in order to draw our attention so that we may give heed to it.

Daniel trembled and lost his bodily strength, until he became like a corrupt dead man without life... God does not want this extreme weakness for us, His children, but He allows it for us if there is benefit in it. For sometimes, when we are in full health, we pay no heed to the divine voice, and we do not enjoy an inner heavenly vision; therefore He allows us bodily weakness for a time, to draw our inner energies to a certain heavenly message. Though the vision terrified Daniel, the heavenly voice gave him reassurance and peace, and the touches of His hand filled him with strength.

10 And, behold, an hand touched me, which set me upon my knees and upon the palms of my hands. 11 And he said unto me, O Daniel, a man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak unto thee, and stand upright: for unto thee am I now sent. And when he had spoken this word unto me, I stood trembling. 12 Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words. 13 But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia. 14 Now I am come to make thee understand what shall befall thy people in the latter days: for yet the vision is for many days.
"And, behold, an hand touched me, which set me upon my knees and upon the palms of my hands" [10].
It is clear that Daniel beheld the vision while prostrate on the ground, and he was leaning on his knees and hands, and he needed heavenly help to raise him up.

The hand that wrote on the wall and terrified king Belshazzar is the one that touched Daniel and gave him strength to rise and to enjoy understanding. Some see that the heavenly hand signifies the divine Incarnation, in which the Lord Christ presented to us the divine work, granting us understanding and wisdom together with redemption and glory.
St. Jerome says: [The angel appeared in the form of a man and laid his hand on the prophet as he lay on the ground. He took on his (human) form so that he would not be terrified!].

The appearing of angels in the form of men reveals heaven's esteem for us as human beings, for although they do not bear bodies like ours, they do not disdain to appear in human form. By this also they declare the longing of the heavenly ones to enter into friendship with us.
"And he said unto me, O Daniel, a man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak unto thee, and stand upright: for unto thee am I now sent.
And when he had spoken this word unto me, I stood trembling" [11].

The hand touched him and a heavenly voice called him, urging him to rise, removing fear from him and granting him understanding. Yet when Daniel rose he was trembling. It is as though God, out of His love for us, allows some weakness to remain in us so that we may not become proud. Daniel alone was qualified for the grace of visions in his time, and he received divine help when God sent him the archangel Gabriel to touch him with his hand, speak with him, and give him understanding. Yet he remained in trembling, so that he realized, with Abraham the father of fathers, that he was dust and ashes.

A heavenly hand touched Daniel and raised him up; perhaps it was the hand of the archangel Gabriel, who interprets the visions to Daniel (Dan 9:23), the one who calls Daniel "greatly beloved", to encourage him and support him.
St. Jerome comments on the expression "beloved", saying: [It is a fitting expression, for every saint carries beauty in himself, and is beloved of the Lord.]
The aged prophet stood, but he was terrified. The angel reassured him that his prayer had been heard and the answer had been sent.

"Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words" [12].

The archangel asked Daniel not to fear, and this was not within Daniel's power, but he needed divine help that would give his mind peace and prepare his depths to grasp the divine mysteries. By saying, "Fear not", he does not offer merely a heavenly commandment, but a heavenly gift that God Himself grants to those who love Him. As for why these gifts were given to Daniel and not to those around him, is there partiality with God? Far from it! Daniel set his heart to understand, and that by prayer, fasting, and humbling himself with repentance. Daniel enjoyed free divine gifts, but not while being negligent in his life, living not in a spirit of luxury and indulgence but in a spirit of earnestness, taking refuge in God, the giver of understanding and knowledge. And as the beloved St. John says, we know that if we ask anything according to His will, He heareth us (1 Jn 5:14).

Daniel humbled himself with repentance before God his God, that is, through a personal relationship with God, whom he reckons as his God, that is, he ascribes Him to himself, and for this reason he was qualified for God to send his angel to him, for the angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him (Ps 145:19).
"But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia" [13].

The angel explains the reason for his delay of 21 days, or three weeks, which were the weeks in which Daniel the prophet was fasting and humbling himself before God, but Daniel did not know this until the three weeks were completed; the angel was working on behalf of the prophet without his knowing.

We often think that God does not hear our prayers or is slow to answer, whereas He cares for us, and hides from us His work on our behalf until we discover it at the proper time, when we become able to understand God's plan and His work for us.
"Now I am come to make thee understand what shall befall thy people in the latter days: for yet the vision is for many days" [14].

The angel assures Daniel that he came to declare to him that his prayers had been answered, and that he was working on behalf of the people, resisting the evil of the king of Persia. He returned to declare to him that God's care extends through many years; he must wait to see by the spirit of prophecy the events to come, not only until the day of his repose, but even to the coming of the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world.
* Let him who doubts that his prayer will be answered be assured that he will not be answered.

Yet we must not ask God anxiously, as the blessed Daniel teaches us, for God heard him from the first day on which he began to offer prayer, but he received the fruit of his prayer after 21 days. So let us not grow slack in the zeal of the prayers we have begun, if we imagine that the answer has been delayed, lest the answer that divine providence grants us be postponed... And this is what could have happened in the case of the prophet mentioned, had he not been found persevering constantly and steadfastly in his prayers during the 21 days although the answer had been issued from the first day.

Abba Isaac The archangel Gabriel explained the secret of his delay in answering his prayer, for he had been resisting "the prince of the kingdom of Persia" for three weeks, until the archangel Michael came, the intercessor for the people of God and a helper to him. What does he mean by the prince of the kingdom of Persia? Does he mean the king or an evil angel resisting the work of God?

An evil angel directed by Satan to tempt the kings of Persia and influence them against the people of God; therefore the angel Gabriel stood, supported by the angel Michael, to shatter the works of the enemy of good against the believers. By "the prince of the kingdom of Persia" he does not mean here a man but Satan, who tempts the king of Persia and moves him.

St. Jerome says: [In my opinion he is the angel entrusted with Persia, as it is written in Deuteronomy: "When the Most High divided to the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the angels" (Deut 32:8). There are the principalities of which Paul speaks: "Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect... Which none of the princes (great ones) of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:6-8). Thus the prince or angel of Persia offered resistance, working on behalf of the province entrusted to him so that the whole captive nation might not be set free. Perhaps although God had graciously heard the prophet from the day he set his heart to understand, yet He did not send the angel to him to declare God's decision, which was full of tenderness, because the angel of Persia resisted him for 21 days, enumerating the sins of the Jewish people as a just basis for their remaining in captivity and as an argument that they should not be set free].

Was the archangel Gabriel unable to resist Satan, who was instilling a spirit of violence and hatred against the believers in Cambyses? Or was he unable to resist the wicked king himself? Why was the angel Michael sent to him? I do not think that the angel's speech here lessens the stature of the angel Gabriel or his power; rather, it reveals the spirit of collective work even among the heavenly ones, and it also declares God's concern for His people, for He sends not one archangel but more for the sake of His people. Jonathan says: "for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few" (1 Sam 14:6). And Asa says: "LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power" (2 Chr 14:11).

The archangel Gabriel affirms that his role had not yet ended, but God left him with the king of Persia, who still bore hatred against the people. For God in His justice did not end the life of the king of Persia, nor did He compel him to love the believers, but left him the freedom of will to do as he pleases; yet for the sake of the believers He sends angels to repel the attacks that come upon them from the wicked king.
In Jewish tradition, as in Christian, the archangel Michael is regarded as a guardian of the people of God (Dan 12:1).

15 And when he had spoken such words unto me, I set my face toward the ground, and I became dumb. 16 And, behold, one like the similitude of the sons of men touched my lips: then I opened my mouth, and spake, and said unto him that stood before me,

O my lord, by the vision my sorrows are turned upon me, and I have retained no strength. 17 For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? for as for me, straightway there remained no strength in me, neither is there breath left in me [15-17].

St. Jerome comments on these words, saying: [It is fitting for our inner nature to direct its gaze outward (and so see that we are in weakness) before it is qualified to behold the vision of God; but once the vision of God is truly realized, our inner nature turns inward and we become wholly numbered among those of whom it is written in another psalm: "The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold" (Ps 44:14)].

Since Daniel was overcome by weakness again, he fell to the ground. And God graciously cared for him, but Daniel was unable to speak until the Lord opened his lips, having made His angel touch his lips...

Although Daniel was unable to enter into a dialogue, the angel supported him, not only with encouraging words and the revealing of the answer to his prayers, but also by his touch. It is as though God affirms to us His longing that we meet with the heavenly ones and enter with them into fellowship of love, for we gather together to praise Him forever.

The angel appeared to him in the likeness of the sons of men so that Daniel might hear him and touch him. In a love full of humility the angels appear to us in the likeness of men, not in respect of their nature but in respect of their form. By contrast, in pride Satan tries to deceive us by appearing in the form of an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14).
Some see that the one who appeared in the likeness of the sons of men is the Word of God, who touched us with His divine love and gave us strength to enter with Him into an open dialogue.

18 Then there came again and touched me one like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me, 19 And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong. And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me. 20 Then said he, Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee? and now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia: and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come. 21 But I will shew thee that which is noted in the scripture of truth: and there is none that holdeth with me in these things, but Michael your prince.
"Then there came again and touched me one like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me,
And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not:
peace be unto thee,
be strong, yea, be strong.
And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me" [18-19].

St. Jerome says: [Had the angel not reassured him by touching him as the son of man, freeing his heart from terror, he could not have heard the secrets of God. For this reason he now says: "Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me", for you have made me able to hear and understand what you say].

Daniel needed a continual heavenly work, for the angel touched him again, and then strengthened him, assuring him that he is a man greatly beloved by God and the heavenly ones, giving him peace and strengthening him with the divine commandment: "be strong, yea, be strong".

We need constant spiritual growth, through our continual meeting with God and our constant enjoyment of fellowship with the heavenly ones and the saints. We touch them, and are strengthened by the living collective work, and we listen to the promises and commandments of God which they utter, that we may be strengthened.
Our life in Christ is a constant enjoyment and an unceasing experience; it is not the product of a certain moment without growth!
When the angel spoke with him and he was strengthened, Daniel was not content with that, but asked for more, saying: "Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me".
"Then said he, Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee?
and now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia" [20].

* What he means is this: Indeed I came to teach you the things you receive as an answer to prayer, but behold, I am going back again to wrestle with the prince of Persia in the eyes of God, because he does not want to set your people free from captivity.
St. Jerome "and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come.
But I will shew thee that which is noted in the scripture of truth:
and there is none that holdeth with me in these things, but Michael your prince" [21].

The Lord sent the angel (perhaps Gabriel) to Daniel, where he spoke with him about a second prince; here he speaks about the Greeks. He also declared that Satan sends his evil angels to stir up the nations to evil, and he acts according to a well-ordered plan.

The angel assured him of the existence of a divine, heavenly plan which God keeps, and declares to us gradually. And that God has entrusted to the archangel Michael the protection of His people against the powers of the devil and his evil angels.

God had sent him to the Persian king Cambyses, but his mission had not yet ended, for the resistance continues in the days of Greece as in the days of Persia; therefore He leaves him to work among the kings who oppose the truth for the sake of protecting the simple believers. It is as though God's care for His Church, by every means, does not cease through the generations, and His sending of His angels continues because the powers of evil do not cease.
Reveal to me Your glory in the midst of my sufferings!
* Grant me, O Lord, with Daniel the spirit of prayer with fasting in humility.
Grant me not to seek pleasant food, but to find in meeting with You my peace and the joy of my heart!
Let me confess my sins and the sins of my people with my tears, for the voice of my tears rises to the throne of Your grace!

* Many times I have thought that You had forgotten me, that You heed not my prayers and the cries of my soul. Uncover my eyes that I may see You working for me; You hide Your works from me for a time, so that my soul may not cease from dialogue with You!
* I have fallen and been terrified; touch me with Your hand, O Holy One, let me hear Your voice that fills me with hope.
Say to me: Be strong, yea, be strong!
Your words have authority over my depths!
* I see the world resisting the truth and persecuting Your Church.
And I see Gabriel, the archangel of Your angels, working together with the great Michael!
You leave to the wicked the fullness of their freedom to act, and in Your love You send Your heavenly soldiers to protect us!
You are wonderful in Your justice as in Your love.
Reveal to me Your glory in the midst of my sufferings!

1 Also I in the first year of Darius the Mede, even I, stood to confirm and to strengthen him. 2 And now will I shew thee the truth. Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia.
"Also I in the first year of Darius the Mede, even I, stood to confirm and to strengthen him" [1].

Some think that the talk here is of the archangel Michael supporting the archangel Gabriel, but this is not acceptable here. Rather the speaker is the archangel Gabriel, who stood beside Darius the king and strengthened him in order to support Cyrus king of Persia against Babylon. In other words, if some kings of Persia resisted God in His people, the victories they gained were by divine permission, and by a power given to them through the angels of God. Here the angel does not boast of his own power and abilities, but speaks as God's agent, and in the name of God who works through His angels.
"And now will I shew thee the truth.
Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia" [2].

The aim of the prophecies in this chapter, which concern the two kingdoms of Persia and Greece and then the conflict between Egypt and Syria, is not to review future events that would arouse the prophet's curiosity, but to declare God's care for His Church and to urge the believers to rely on God and trust in His divine providence even in critical moments. Indeed, outwardly there appear to be worldwide conflicts between the great powers such as Babylon, Persia, Media, and Greece, and between the two halves of the Greek empire, namely the state of the Ptolemies and the state of the Seleucids; but behind these events is the hidden hand of God, who turns the whole course of affairs to the building up of His Church, and God gives His covenant with His people a special priority even if no one notices it.

Although this whole prophecy was given in the third year of Cyrus (Dan 10:1), the archangel Gabriel referred earlier to when he secretly confirmed Darius and strengthened him in his first year. This probably happened at the time when Daniel was cast into the den.

Some see that the three kings who reigned in Persia after Cyrus are: 1. Cambyses the son of Cyrus (527-522 BC): while he was on a long mission in Egypt, his younger brother Magus, surnamed Smerdis, was assassinated. 2. The so-called Smerdis (522-521 BC): he usurped the kingdom after the assassination of Smerdis, and resembled Smerdis in appearance; he married Pantaptes the daughter of Cambyses. He remained in power for 7 months and seven Magi assassinated him. 3. Darius Hystaspes or Darius I (521-486 BC) became king, and he married the same Pantaptes, the wife of the previous king, and she bore him Ahasuerus (Xerxes), who became one of the richest and most famous kings.
Others see that by the three kings the angel means Cyrus, his son Cambyses, and Darius, excluding the deceitful usurper "the so-called Smerdis".

The archangel spoke of a fourth king who surpassed the three previous kings in wealth, namely Ahasuerus the son of Darius (480-465 BC), who married Esther. St. Justin speaks of his wealth, saying that he had so many riches that even if the rivers were dried up by his forces, his wealth would not be exhausted. He crossed with an army numbering 2,641,000 persons and conquered the Greeks. The Greeks set it in their heart to avenge themselves, and they did so. He remained four years gathering his army, but the excessive size of the army deprived him of the ability to organize it, and he was defeated in the battle of Salamis. Through his pride and impetuosity Ahasuerus was defeated, and fled in a small boat, and found not one ship to rescue him, although the waters of the sea were covered with his huge fleet which he lost through his poor organization. His people counted him foolish in his military conduct, and they also despised him because he killed his brother, behaved shamefully with his sister, and committed other crimes.

The angel regarded the rest of the kings of Persia as being like those who fell. For the state of Persia declined and the spirit of the people was shattered, and the kings afterwards became as though they had no existence until Alexander the Macedonian dominated the world.

St. Jerome says: [It must be noted that after the book enumerated some of the kings of Persia after Cyrus, it clearly omitted the nine other kings and passed directly to Alexander, because the spirit of prophecy is not concerned with presenting historical details, but presents briefly only the most important events].

3 And a mighty king shall stand up, that shall rule with great dominion, and do according to his will. 4 And when he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken, and shall be divided toward the four winds of heaven; and not to his posterity, nor according to his dominion which he ruled: for his kingdom shall be plucked up, even for others beside those. [3-4].

He indicates quite clearly that at the proper time Alexander the Great (356-323 BC) will arise and with great power defeat Persia and other states. We have already spoken of the enmity that Alexander the Great bore toward the Jews, but on his way to Judea he saw a vision which was fulfilled when he saw the high priest in his priestly garments receiving him with great hospitality and presenting to him the prophecies of Daniel the prophet, to assure him that he would defeat Persia and establish a great kingdom. Thereby his enmity turned into friendship, and he treated the Jews well.

He died suddenly in Babylon after successive and swift conquests and victories, but he became drunk with extreme success and wealth, and died while intoxicated. No one knows whether he died of an illness that struck him suddenly while he was drunk, for which no cure was known, or died poisoned, whether he drank the poison to commit suicide or Cassander hid it for him. The angel's saying "And when he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken" means that after he became the sole king of the whole East, his kingdom collapsed through his sudden death. We have already spoken of the conflicts and assassinations that took place after his death until his kingdom was finally divided among four of his commanders after the battle of Ipsus.

He says: "for his kingdom shall be plucked up, even for others beside those" [4]. This prophecy was fulfilled precisely and literally, for none of his sons inherited the throne, nor any of his relatives, but foreign commanders took the throne, although he had two sons, Heracleus and Alexander II, but neither of them took the rule; rather they were killed, one before his father's death and the other after it.

St. Jerome says: [Besides the four kingdoms, that is, Macedonia, Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt, the kingdom of the Macedonians was torn among other, less important rulers and among petty kings of no standing. Here he refers to Perdiccas, Lysimachus, Craterus, and others who ruled Cappadocia, Armenia, Bithynia, Heraclea, Bosphorus, and many other regions that withdrew from Macedonian power and set up different kings for themselves].
All this the angel declared to Daniel the prophet many years before the birth of Alexander the Great.

entries.section: 3. Prophecies about the conflict between Egypt and Syria:

paragraphs.text: 5 And the king of the south shall be strong, and one of his princes; and he shall be strong above him, and have dominion; his dominion shall be a great dominion. 6 And in the end of years they shall join themselves together; for the king's daughter of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement: but she shall not retain the power of the arm; neither shall he stand, nor his arm: but she shall be given up, and they that brought her, and he that begat her, and he that strengthened her in these times. 7 But out of a branch of her roots shall one stand up in his estate, which shall come with an army, and shall enter into the fortress of the king of the north, and shall deal against them, and shall prevail: 8 And shall also carry captives into Egypt their gods, with their molten images, and with their precious vessels of silver and of gold; and he shall refrain some years from the king of the north. 9 So the king of the south shall come into his kingdom, and shall return into his own land. 10 But his sons shall be stirred up, and shall assemble a multitude of great forces: and one shall certainly come, and overflow, and pass through: then shall he return, and be stirred up, even to his fortress. 11 And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand. 12 And when he hath taken away the multitude, his heart shall be lifted up; and he shall cast down many ten thousands: but he shall not be strengthened by it. 13 For the king of the north shall return, and shall set forth a multitude greater than the former, and shall certainly come after certain years with a great army and with much riches. 14 And in those times there shall many stand up against the king of the south: also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; but they shall stumble. 15 So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither shall there be any strength to withstand. 16 But he that cometh against him shall do according to his own will, and none shall stand before him: and he shall stand in the glorious land, which shall be wholly in his hand. 17 He shall also set his face to enter with the strength of his whole kingdom, and shall make peace with him; and he shall give him the daughter of women, corrupting her: but she shall not stand on his side, neither be for him. 18 After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many: and a prince shall cause his reproach to cease, and moreover shall turn his reproach back upon him. 19 Then he shall turn his face toward the fort of his own land: but he shall stumble and fall, and not be found. 20 Then shall stand up in his estate one that causeth an exactor of tribute to pass through the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle. 21 And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come suddenly, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries. 22 And the arms of the flood shall be swept away from before him, and shall be broken; so also the prince of the covenant. 23 And after the league made with him he shall work deceitfully: for he shall come up, and shall become strong with a small people. 24 He shall enter suddenly upon the fattest places of the land; and he shall do that which his fathers have not done, nor his fathers' fathers; he shall scatter among them the prey, and spoil, and riches: yea, and he shall forecast his devices against the strong holds, even for a time. 25 And he shall stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south shall be stirred up to battle with a very great and mighty army; but he shall not stand: for they shall forecast devices against him. 26 Yea, they that feed of the portion of his meat shall destroy him, and his army shall overflow: and many shall fall down slain. 27 And both these kings' hearts shall be to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table; but it shall not prosper: for yet the end shall be at the time appointed. 28 Then shall he return into his land with great riches; and his heart shall be against the holy covenant; and he shall do exploits, and return to his own land. 29 At the time appointed he shall return, and come toward the south; but it shall not be as the former, or as the latter. 30 For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall despair, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; he shall even return, and have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant. 31 And arms shall stand on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and shall take away the daily sacrifice, and they shall place the abomination that maketh desolate. 32 And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits. 33 And they that understand among the people shall instruct many: yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days. 34 Now when they shall fall, they shall be holpen with a little help: but many shall cleave to them with flatteries. 35 And some of them of understanding shall fall, to try them, and to purge, and to make them white, even to the time of the end: because it is yet for a time appointed.

These prophecies speak of the wars of the Seleucids with the Ptolemies, for these two dynasties entered into perpetual wars against one another. By virtue of the geographical position of Palestine, in the middle between Egypt and Syria, it was in most cases the battlefield for both sides. The kings of Egypt were called the kings of the south, and the kings of Syria the kings of the north.

It is fitting for us to realize that this section covers a long period of time, about two centuries, and when it speaks of the king of the north or the king of the south it does not mean one particular king for each of the two states.
"And the king of the south shall be strong,
and one of his princes; and he shall be strong above him, and have dominion; his dominion shall be a great dominion" [5].

The first king of the south (Egypt) was strong, he and his wife; he was Ptolemy Lagus (the First, 323-285 BC). He was strong, intelligent, and rich, stronger than Antiochus the son of Seleucus, king of the north (Syria), but afterwards Antiochus became stronger and richer, since he annexed Babylonia and Media. The angel knew the greatness that Antiochus would attain, more than Ptolemy, in the future.
As for who is meant by one of his princes who became stronger than he and had greater dominion, St. Jerome says of him:

[The person mentioned here is Ptolemy Philadelphus, the second king of Egypt, and the son of the Ptolemy previously mentioned. It is said that in his reign the seventy translated the Holy Bible into Greek.
He also sent many treasures to Jerusalem to Eleazar the high priest, and sent vessels for the Temple.
The keeper of his library was Demetrius of Phalrum, a man of fame among the Greeks as an orator and philosopher.

It is reported of Philadelphus that he was of great power which surpassed that of his father Ptolemy, for history relates of him that he had 200,000 foot soldiers, twenty thousand horsemen, two thousand chariots, and four hundred elephants, the first to import them from Ethiopia...
His treasure of gold and silver was very great, and his annual income which he received from Egypt amounted to 14,800 pieces of silver, and the wheat from half a million to a million ardebs].

"And in the end of years they shall join themselves together; for the king's daughter of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement: but she shall not retain the power of the arm; neither shall he stand, nor his arm: but she shall be given up, and they that brought her, and he that begat her, and he that strengthened her in these times" [6].

He prophesies of the latter days, when a treaty was made between the kings of Egypt and Syria in 250 BC, and the means of this treaty was the marriage of the king of Syria to the daughter of the king of Egypt. Indeed, Antiochus Theos (285-247 BC), the third king of Syria, divorced his wife Laodice to marry Berenice, or Betonice, or Bernice, the daughter of Ptolemy II (283-246 BC), the one called Philadelphus. He gave his daughter thousands of pieces of gold and silver without number as a dowry for her, so that he was called Phernophoros, that is, "the dowry-giver" Dowery-giver (dotalis). Ptolemy's aim was to use the marriage of his daughter to the king of Syria as an opportunity to gain control over Syria and the whole kingdom of Antiochus, but the plan failed. For Laodice, whom Antiochus kept after divorcing her as one of his concubines and not as queen, stirred up her friends against the king, and killed her rival Berenice and those around her. Antiochus took back his first wife Laodice, who, it is said, killed him by poison shortly afterward, and she set her elder son Seleucus Callinicus on the throne, and the younger son, Antiochus the Younger, called Hierax, as governor over Asia Minor. It is said that the elder son was the one who won over Berenice and promised her that he would care for her, so she was reassured by him, and he killed her and her son in a vile and hideous way. Thus, since deceit entered the lives of the two kings, both failed.

The prophecy was fulfilled literally, for the plan of the king of Egypt failed completely: on the one hand the king did not attain his goal by giving his daughter as wife to the king of Syria, and the daughter was killed along with those around her, and also her husband who had been her support, and her son was killed as well.

"But out of a branch of her roots shall one stand up in his estate, which shall come with an army, and shall enter into the fortress of the king of the north, and shall deal against them, and shall prevail:
And shall also carry captives into Egypt their gods, with their molten images, and with their precious vessels of silver and of gold;
and he shall refrain some years from the king of the north.
So the king of the south shall come into his kingdom, and shall return into his own land" [7-9].

He indicates that a branch of the family of Bernice will come and defeat the king of the north. Indeed, Ptolemy (III) Euergetes, the brother of Berenice, probably younger than she, the third king of Egypt who succeeded his father Philadelphus, gathered a great army to avenge his sister. And indeed he defeated Callinicus, who was ruling Syria jointly with his mother Laodice, and conquered many fortified cities. He not only triumphed over Syria, but also stormed Cilicia and some regions beyond the Euphrates, and almost gained dominion over all of Asia. News came of a rebellion arising in Egypt, which made Euergetes hasten back to Egypt carrying with him the captives and also two and a half thousand statues of gold and silver, some of which Cambyses had brought from Egypt long before, and he also carried 40,000 talents of silver. Callinicus did not think of entering into another battle with Euergetes, for he knew that he could not defeat him or recover what he had carried off as spoil. Euergetes remained king for 46 years [8]. When Callinicus felt defeated before Euergetes he appealed for help to his brother Hierax, governor of Asia Minor, who paid no heed to his brother's cries, for he reckoned that he was more entitled to the throne. Later he entered into a battle with his brother, and his brother fell dead from his horse, while Euergetes remained king in Egypt for 4 years after the death of the king of Syria. In any case Euergetes did not return to Syria.

"But his sons shall be stirred up, and shall assemble a multitude of great forces: and one shall certainly come, and overflow, and pass through: then shall he return, and be stirred up, even to his fortress.

And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand" [10-11].

He prophesies of the two sons of Callinicus king of Syria, Seleucus (II) Ceraunus and Antiochus the Great, who gathered an army to take revenge on the Egyptians after the death of Euergetes. But Ceraunus was killed in Phrygia in the third year of his reign, betrayed by Nicanor and Apaturius while he was preparing for the battle against Egypt, leaving the rule to his brother alone. Antiochus the Great became a distinguished king and led a huge army against Egypt. At that time Ptolemy Philopator was the fourth king of Egypt, and he bore the title Philopator as a mark of disgrace, because the word means "lover of his father", while he killed his father, his mother, and his brother, so the people hated him. This is what drove Antiochus the Great to enter with him into a fierce battle at Raphia in 217 BC, in which both sides used huge elephants, to recover what Syria had lost, regarding the people's hatred of their king as an opportunity for victory. But the king of Egypt gathered a great army almost equal to the army of Syria. Ceraunus was able to move with his army and recover the seized Syrian lands, while the king of Egypt, characterized by cowardice and negligence, was preparing with his great army, and when he met the army of Antiochus he defeated it in a great slaughter [11].
Philopator did not defeat Antiochus the Great by his courage and strength, but the Lord permitted this to break the pride of the latter.
And since he was negligent in following up his victory, especially as he did not trust those around him, in spite of his victory he made peace with Antiochus in an ungenerous manner [12].
"And when he hath taken away the multitude, his heart shall be lifted up; and he shall cast down many ten thousands: but he shall not be strengthened by it" [12].

The historians say that Philopator could easily have seized Syria, but he was given over to his bodily lusts and the dissolution of his character, along with his committing many crimes. For on his return from the war he killed his wife Eurydice and committed many crimes, and he also handed the reins of the kingdom to a wicked woman, a musician called Agathoclea, and he fell in love with her brother Agathocles, whom he set up as commander-in-chief over Egypt.

After he became famous for victories, so that the whole East feared him, he plunged into drunkenness with idleness and slackness, and nothing occupied him any longer except banquets, revels, and pleasures; thereby his heart was lifted up to the clouds of his victories, only to fall cast down in shame.
"For the king of the north shall return, and shall set forth a multitude greater than the former, and shall certainly come after certain years with a great army and with much riches.
And in those times there shall many stand up against the king of the south: also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; and they exult" [13-14].

Here the angel declares to the prophet the rise of new wars, for after the death of Ptolemy Philopator, Egypt was without a king, since his son Ptolemy Epiphanes (the Fifth, 203-181 BC) was a small child four years old, and the perversion and arrogance of Agathocles increased greatly, so the provinces subject to Egypt rose up and rebelled against the rule, and entered into great internal troubles. Antiochus attacked Egypt, and since Egypt had become very weak it sent an embassy to Rome, and since the Romans desired to extend their dominion in the world, they sent to Antiochus asking him to stop the war. After many attempts he failed in his war, and finally he triumphed in a battle against the Egyptian commander Scopas on the border of Judea. The angel made clear that Antiochus the Great did not stand alone against Egypt, but Egypt came to have many enemies.
Antiochus made a treaty with Philip III of Macedon, and asked the help of the Jews [13]. The pious among the Jews refused to help him, but some Jews supported him.

What do we mean by the robbers of the people of Daniel who exalt themselves to establish the vision? St. Jerome sees in this a prophecy about the high priest Onias the Younger, who betrayed the altar of the Lord and defiled it in Jerusalem. He fled to Egypt taking with him a great number of Jews, and Ptolemy received him with great honor. The king gave him the region of Heliopolis (New Egypt), and there he built an altar to the Lord, claiming that he was fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet concerning the setting up of an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt (Isa 19:19), as the Book of Maccabees tells us and also the historian Josephus. St. Jerome says: [The temple remained standing until the time of Vespasian for 250 years. The city itself was called "the city of Onias", and it was destroyed during the war between the Jews and the Romans. No trace of the temple or of the city remained in the days of St. Jerome.

"So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither shall there be any strength to withstand.
But he that cometh against him shall do according to his own will, and none shall stand before him: and he shall stand in the glorious land, which shall be wholly in his hand.

He shall also set his face to enter with the strength of his whole kingdom, and shall make peace with him; and he shall give him the daughter of women, corrupting her: but she shall not stand on his side, neither be for him" [15-17].

St. Jerome says that Antiochus, in order to recover Judea and some cities of Syria, entered into a battle with Scopas, the commander of Ptolemy, beside the Jordan near a city called Peneas, and Scopas fled, but he was besieged in Sidon with ten thousand of his soldiers. The Egyptians no longer had strength to resist, and so he sat in the glorious land, Palestine, which came under his dominion; in the Septuagint it reads "the land of desire", by which is meant the land in which God delights. God had declared beforehand to Daniel what would happen, so that when Palestine fell into the hands of the violent Antiochus, the spirit of the pious would not be shattered, but they would realize that God had declared this beforehand. Thus this prophecy becomes a cause of comfort to them in the midst of distress and of falling under suffering and persecution. And in order to bring Egypt into his grasp, Antiochus gave his beautiful daughter Cleopatra to the young Ptolemy, thinking that by this he would subject Egypt to his dominion. But she did not stand by him [17], but stood by her husband, so he turned his face from Egypt to Asia Minor with his naval fleet and captured many of the isles.
"After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many: and a prince shall cause his reproach to cease, and moreover shall turn his reproach back upon him" [18].

By the isles are meant Asia Minor, the coasts of the Mediterranean, Greece, Cyprus, and all the islands in the sea. For it was the custom of the Jews to call all the regions lying beyond the sea "isles", since they had no experience of maritime affairs.

Antiochus was able, with a small army, to advance into Asia Minor, and with him was Hannibal, whose fame had reached the Romans and who were terrified of him, so it was not difficult for him to drive the Romans out of every region he crossed into. Hannibal became an intimate friend of Antiochus, accompanying him every day and speaking with him, but Antiochus doubted his loyalty. Antiochus headed toward Greece without good planning and without caution, and when he reached Chalcis he was attracted to a beautiful girl there and held a wedding feast with her as though he were in his own land in perfect peace. By virtue of his great fame he opened many cities that were terrified before him, and freed these cities from the Romans. And as the angel declares to Daniel: "After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many" [18].

By rejecting the counsel of Hannibal, Antiochus began to collapse and disgrace came upon him without his knowing, and he mocked the Romans and reproached them. He first occupied some regions in Greece that were allied with the newly emerging Roman power, but the Roman commander Acilius, or Lucius Scipio Nasica (with his brother Publius Scipio Aficanus), was able to draw him beyond Mount Taurus and defeat him at Magnesia, and so he turned back on Antiochus the reproaches that he used to utter against the Romans; therefore the angel declares "and a prince shall cause his reproach to cease, and moreover shall turn his reproach back upon him" [18]. Thereby Antiochus collapsed before Greece allied with Rome. And here many blame the commander Scipio because he left all the resources of Rome at the disposal of Philip of Macedon.
"Then he shall turn his face toward the fort of his own land: but he shall stumble and fall, and not be found" [19].

Antiochus weakened before the Roman commander Scipio, and returned to his country in disappointment to fortify himself in his land after losing many [19], and when he tried to plunder the temple of Jupiter Dodoneus in Elymais near Susa, perhaps to pay the Roman tribute, he and his soldiers were killed by the people who rose in revolt against him. Therefore the angel says "he shall fall, and not be found".

Antiochus died in 187 BC. After him reigned Seleucus Philopator (187-176 BC), whom some call Ceraunus, and the second son was Demetrius. The third was Antiochus Epiphanes. Now he speaks of his successor Seleucus, saying:
"Then shall stand up in his estate one that causeth an exactor of tribute to pass through the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle?" [20].

His son Seleucus Philopator succeeded him, and he was excessive in demanding taxes [20] to pay the tribute to Rome, so he sent his prime minister Heliodorus to Jerusalem to plunder the Temple there. Soon afterward Heliodorus assassinated his master, and Antiochus Epiphanes took the rule.
"And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come suddenly, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries" [21].

All the historians agree that Antiochus Epiphanes was cunning and violent to the utmost degree. When news of his father's death reached Rome, they released him, since they were content (they made light of) with his brother Demetrius. He flattered the Romans, and when he reached his country they received him with great hospitality. His brother Seleucus did not last long, and had left his son as his successor, but Antiochus by his deceit was able to take the rule without right; therefore the angel says of him: "to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom" and continues "and obtain the kingdom by flatteries". How was that done? By his deceit he pretended to be a man of peace with his nephew, the lawful heir to the kingdom, and that he was his guardian... Thereby he was able to take the kingdom from him.
"And the arms of the flood shall be swept away from before him, and shall be broken; so also the prince of the covenant" [22].

Antiochus found resistance from his own people, who discovered his deceit and his exclusion of his nephew, and he also found trouble from the surrounding countries such as Egypt, for its king Ptolemy Philometor was a boy, and his advisers were on good terms with the son of Seleucus whom his uncle had excluded, so they sent secret help to resist Antiochus. Many neighboring countries did likewise. But all these resisting arms were broken, as the angel says here, for they were like a sweeping flood. Yet they went before him and collapsed. This was not because of the strength of Antiochus but by divine permission, for God permitted his rising to discipline the Jews at that time.
Who is the prince of the covenant who was broken before Antiochus? Ptolemy is meant, because he is related by kinship to the lawful heir, the son of Seleucus.

This Ptolemy Philometor was the son of Ptolemy Philopator and Cleopatra the sister of Seleucus, and although he was a small boy who could not move by himself, he was a prince of the covenant by being king of Egypt.
